terms.shortDef: Randomly splitting live traffic between two versions to compare outcomes.
terms.longDef: Users are assigned at random to variant A or B and a pre-declared metric decides the winner. Randomisation is what buys you causality: any difference that survives is attributable to the change. It needs enough traffic to reach significance, and it can only compare options you already thought of.
terms.example: Half of visitors see a one-step checkout and half see three steps; conversion is compared over two weeks at a pre-agreed sample size.
terms.misuse: Stopping the test the moment it looks significant inflates false positives. Set the duration and sample size before you start.

terms.shortDef: The part of a page visible before any scrolling.
terms.longDef: Borrowed from newspapers, it still matters because what is visible first sets expectations about whether the page is worth continuing. People scroll willingly, so the goal is not cramming everything in but making the top compelling and clearly continuing. The fold is not one line — it differs on every device.
terms.example: Ending a section slightly below the viewport edge so it is obvious there is more, rather than exactly at it.
terms.misuse: "Everything important above the fold" is outdated advice that produces cramped tops and empty pages beneath.

terms.shortDef: The conditions a piece of work must meet to be finished.
terms.longDef: Criteria are written before the work and phrased so that each one is either met or not. For design-heavy work they should include states, responsive behaviour and accessibility requirements, otherwise those become optional. They are how "done" stops being a matter of opinion.
terms.example: "Keyboard focus order follows the visual order" and "error text is announced by a screen reader" as explicit criteria.

terms.shortDef: Making a product usable by people with disabilities.
terms.longDef: Accessibility covers vision, hearing, motor and cognitive differences, permanent and temporary alike. It is a baseline requirement rather than a feature, and in many jurisdictions a legal one. Built in from the start it costs little; retrofitted it is one of the most expensive things a team can do.
terms.example: A form that can be completed with a keyboard, announced correctly by a screen reader, and read at 200% text size.
terms.misuse: "a11y" is a numeronym — eleven letters between the a and the y — not an abbreviation to say aloud as a word.

terms.shortDef: A structured assessment against a standard such as WCAG.
terms.longDef: An audit combines automated scanning, manual keyboard and screen-reader testing, and judgement about criteria that cannot be automated. The output is a prioritised list of failures with the criterion each breaches. Testing with disabled users is a separate and complementary activity — an audit finds standard violations, not lived friction.
terms.example: A report listing each failure, the WCAG criterion, the screens affected and a suggested fix, ranked by severity.
terms.misuse: An automated scan reporting zero issues is not a passed audit. Most criteria cannot be checked by a tool.

terms.shortDef: The text assistive technology announces for an element.
terms.longDef: It comes from the visible label where there is one, and otherwise from an explicit attribute. Names must describe the outcome — "Save term", not "button" or "icon" — and should include the visible text so voice-control users can say what they see. Every interactive element needs one.
terms.example: An icon-only close control given the name "Close settings" rather than being announced as an unlabelled button.
terms.misuse: Adding a name that differs from the visible label breaks voice control, which matches on what is on screen.

terms.shortDef: Stacked sections that expand one at a time to reveal content.
terms.longDef: Accordions compress a long page into scannable headings, letting people open only what they need. They work when the headings are genuinely self-describing and the sections are independent. They hurt when users need to compare sections, or when the content inside is what everyone came for.
terms.example: A product page collapsing delivery, returns and materials into three headings, with none open by default.
terms.misuse: Collapsing content people always read adds a tap for everyone. Measure before hiding.

terms.shortDef: The point where a new user first gets real value.
terms.longDef: Activation is defined by finding the early action that best predicts retention, then measuring how many new users reach it and how long it takes. It gives onboarding a target more useful than completion of a tour. The action has to be genuine value, not a proxy the team finds convenient to count.
terms.example: Users who look up three terms in their first session retain far better, so that becomes the activation event.

terms.shortDef: People perceive attractive designs as easier to use.
terms.longDef: A polished interface is judged more usable than a plain one, even when both perform identically, and users forgive more of its small problems. That is genuinely valuable, and it is also a trap in research: a beautiful prototype can mask usability problems that only surface once it ships. Watch behaviour, not praise.
terms.example: Participants rate a well-typeset form as simpler than an unstyled one, while taking the same time to complete both.
terms.misuse: It does not mean visual polish substitutes for usability. It means polish hides the evidence.

terms.shortDef: Grouping raw observations into themes to find patterns.
terms.longDef: Every observation goes on its own note, then notes that belong together are clustered and the clusters are named. The naming is the analysis — it forces you to say what the group actually means. Done with the team, it also spreads the findings faster than any report.
terms.example: Two hundred notes from eight interviews collapse into six themes, one of which is "people do not trust the estimated delivery date".
terms.misuse: Clustering by feature area rather than by what participants were experiencing turns analysis into a backlog sort.

terms.shortDef: What an object makes possible for the person using it.
terms.longDef: An affordance is a relationship between a thing and someone who can act on it: a handle affords pulling, a flat plate affords pushing. In screen design the relevant version is the perceived affordance — whether the person can tell the action is available. Something can afford tapping and still fail, if nothing signals it.
terms.example: A raised, rounded rectangle with a label reads as pressable; the same words as plain grey text do not.
terms.misuse: Often used to mean the visual cue itself. The cue is the signifier; the affordance is the possibility of the action.

terms.shortDef: Delivering software in short cycles with frequent feedback.
terms.longDef: Agile methods favour working software, close collaboration and responding to change over long upfront specification. For designers the challenge is that two-week cycles suit building better than they suit discovery, which is why research usually runs a cycle ahead. Most organisations practise a partial version shaped by their existing structure.
terms.example: Design works one sprint ahead on the next flow while engineering builds the one validated last sprint.
terms.misuse: Agile is not "no documentation" or "no plan". It is a preference between competing goods, not the abolition of one of them.

terms.shortDef: A system that plans and takes actions to reach a goal.
terms.longDef: Agents chain model calls with tools — searching, writing files, calling APIs — to pursue an objective across several steps. The design problems are consent and legibility: what the agent may do without asking, how progress is shown, and how a user stops or reverses it. Irreversible actions taken on a user's behalf need explicit confirmation.
terms.example: An assistant that drafts replies and queues them, requiring one confirmation before anything is sent.

terms.shortDef: Systematic unfairness in a system's outputs across groups.
terms.longDef: Bias enters through training data that reflects historical inequity, through proxies that stand in for protected characteristics, and through evaluation that only measures the average case. It surfaces as worse performance for accents, skin tones, names or dialects outside the majority. Testing has to be disaggregated by group, because an aggregate accuracy figure hides it completely.
terms.example: Speech input with materially higher error rates for some regional accents, invisible in the overall accuracy number.

terms.shortDef: Lining elements up so the eye reads an intentional edge.
terms.longDef: Shared edges create relationships and calm; stray ones read as errors even when nobody can say why. Optical alignment sometimes overrides mathematical alignment — a circle or a piece of punctuation must sit slightly outside the true edge to look aligned. Fewer alignment lines generally means a stronger layout.
terms.example: A quotation mark hung slightly into the margin so the first letter of the quote lines up with the paragraph below.

terms.shortDef: A text description of an image, for people who cannot see it.
terms.longDef: Good alt text conveys the image's purpose in this context rather than describing every detail — the same photograph needs different alt text in a news story and a shop listing. Purely decorative images should be marked as such so they are skipped entirely. If the image carries information found nowhere else, that information belongs in the text.
terms.example: A chart's alt text states the trend and the key figure, with the full data available in a table beneath it.
terms.misuse: "Image of…" wastes the first two words — screen readers already announce that it is an image.

terms.shortDef: Computing that works in the background without demanding attention.
terms.longDef: Sensors, wearables and connected devices act on context rather than waiting for explicit commands, so the interface is often a light, a sound or nothing at all. The design principles are restraint and legibility: only interrupt when it matters, and make it possible to find out why something happened. Without that, ambient systems feel like haunted houses.
terms.example: Lights that adjust with the room, with a visible log and an override, rather than changing for reasons nobody can inspect.

terms.shortDef: A common solution that reliably makes things worse.
terms.longDef: An anti-pattern is a recurring response to a problem that seems reasonable and produces predictable damage — mystery-meat icons, modal onboarding tours, infinite scroll on search results. Naming them helps teams reject them without re-litigating the reasoning each time. Unlike deceptive patterns, they are usually well intentioned.
terms.example: Replacing labelled navigation with icons alone saves space and reliably reduces the use of every section.
terms.misuse: An anti-pattern is not always wrong. It is wrong often enough that using one needs a reason.

terms.shortDef: A defined way for one piece of software to ask another for something.
terms.longDef: When a designer hears "the API doesn't return that", it means the data needed for a screen is not available in the shape or at the time the design assumes. API limits explain a surprising number of interface compromises: why a count is missing, why a list cannot be sorted that way, why a step needs its own screen. Knowing what the API can do early changes what you design.
terms.example: A design showing total results needs the endpoint to return a count; if it only returns a page, the number cannot be shown.

terms.shortDef: Attributes that describe roles, states and properties to assistive tech.
terms.longDef: ARIA fills gaps where native elements cannot express a pattern — a tab set, a combobox, a live region. It changes what is announced, never what the element does, so keyboard behaviour still has to be built by hand. Misapplied ARIA is worse than none, because it overrides correct native semantics.
terms.example: A custom tab list marked with the tablist, tab and tabpanel roles, plus arrow-key handling written to match.
terms.misuse: Adding role="button" to a div does not make it focusable or operable by keyboard. It only changes the announcement.

terms.shortDef: Software or hardware people use to operate a device.
terms.longDef: Screen readers, magnifiers, switch devices, voice control, braille displays, eye-gaze systems and alternative keyboards all sit between the person and your interface. Each depends on the structure and names your product exposes, not on how it looks. Designing without knowing which technologies your audience uses is guessing.
terms.example: A switch user navigates by scanning through focusable elements, so focus order and visible focus decide whether the app works.

terms.shortDef: Suggesting completions as someone types into a field.
terms.longDef: Autocomplete converts recall into recognition, cuts typing and reduces spelling errors — especially valuable on phones. Suggestions must be ranked usefully, keyboard navigable and announced to assistive technology. Autofill from stored data is a related and even higher-value case.
terms.example: Typing "lond" into a destination field offers London Heathrow and London City, with the airport codes shown.
terms.misuse: Suggestions that replace what the user typed on blur cause silent wrong entries. Never overwrite without a deliberate selection.

terms.shortDef: The ordered list of work a team has not done yet.
terms.longDef: A healthy backlog is ordered rather than merely long, with the top few items understood well enough to start and everything below deliberately vague. Items that have sat untouched for a year are not a backlog, they are a record of things you decided not to do. Deleting them is a feature.
terms.example: The top ten items are refined and estimated; below that sits a rough list nobody has designed yet.

terms.shortDef: People ignore anything that looks like an advert.
terms.longDef: Users learn the visual signature of promotional content — right rail, bright colours, a boxed area at the top — and stop seeing it, whether or not it is actually an ad. Genuine content styled that way disappears with it. The fix is to look like the content, not to shout louder.
terms.example: An important account notice placed in a coloured box in the top right is missed by most users, including in eye-tracking studies.
terms.misuse: Not caused by ads alone. Any repeated decorative block in a predictable slot earns the same treatment.

terms.shortDef: A repeatable measurement of usability, run to compare over time.
terms.longDef: The same tasks, metrics and recruiting criteria are run at intervals so the numbers are comparable. Typical measures are task success, time on task and a standard satisfaction score. The discipline is in keeping the method identical — change the tasks and you have lost the comparison you were building.
terms.example: Every six months the team runs the same five tasks with 30 participants and charts success rate against the previous round.

terms.shortDef: A panel that slides up from the bottom edge, over the content.
terms.longDef: Sheets put options within thumb reach and keep the underlying context partly visible, which makes them a gentler alternative to a full modal on phones. They can be non-modal, letting the page behind stay live. Anything taller than half the screen should probably be a page.
terms.example: Tapping share raises a sheet of destinations without leaving the article behind it.

terms.shortDef: The share of visits that end without a second interaction.
terms.longDef: A high bounce rate can mean the page failed or that it answered the question immediately — a phone number, an opening time, a definition. Interpretation depends entirely on the page's job. On its own it is one of the most misread numbers in analytics.
terms.example: A reference page with a 78% bounce rate and long time on page is probably succeeding, not failing.
terms.misuse: Treating bounce rate as a quality score punishes pages that do their job in one screen.

terms.shortDef: The impression a product leaves, and the system that shapes it.
terms.longDef: Brand is not the logo — it is the accumulated result of everything the product does, of which the visual identity is one part. In interface terms it lives in typography, colour, tone of voice and how the product behaves when something goes wrong. Consistency across those does more for recognition than any single asset.
terms.example: A bank whose error messages are calm, specific and never blame the customer builds more brand than its logo does.

terms.shortDef: A trail showing where a page sits in the hierarchy.
terms.longDef: Breadcrumbs show the path from the top level to the current page and let people jump up a level in one tap. They are most valuable on deep, hierarchical sites and on pages people arrive at from search, with no sense of context. They supplement navigation rather than replacing it.
terms.example: Home › Support › Deliveries › Missing parcel, where every step before the last is tappable.
terms.misuse: A breadcrumb showing the path the user took, rather than the site hierarchy, is a history trail and confuses more than it helps.

terms.shortDef: A width at which the layout changes to a different arrangement.
terms.longDef: Breakpoints should be set where the design stops working, not at the dimensions of particular devices, which change every year. Fewer, well-chosen breakpoints are easier to maintain than many device-specific ones. Container queries increasingly let a component respond to its own space rather than the whole viewport.
terms.example: Adding a second column at the width where the reading measure would otherwise exceed 75 characters.
terms.misuse: Naming breakpoints after phones and tablets ages badly and ignores split-screen and resized desktop windows.

terms.shortDef: Keeping a copy of data so it does not have to be fetched again.
terms.longDef: Caches make things fast and make them stale, and the design question is which of those the user notices. Anything that must be current — a balance, a stock level — needs a visible freshness signal or a way to refresh. Cache invalidation is genuinely hard, which is why "try clearing your cache" persists as advice.
terms.example: Showing cached search results instantly with a quiet "updated 2 minutes ago", refreshing in the background.

terms.shortDef: Synchronised text of speech and meaningful sound in video.
terms.longDef: Captions serve deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, and in practice a large share of all viewers, who watch with sound off. Good captions include speaker changes and important non-speech sound, not just dialogue. Auto-generated captions need editing before they can be relied on, particularly for names and jargon.
terms.example: "[door closes] Priya: I've sent the file" rather than dialogue alone.
terms.misuse: Subtitles assume the viewer can hear and only translate speech; captions do not. The words are not interchangeable.

terms.shortDef: A bounded container grouping one item's content and actions.
terms.longDef: Cards make a set of things scannable by drawing a region around each, and they rearrange easily across screen sizes. They cost vertical space and, used everywhere, flatten hierarchy into a uniform grid where nothing leads. A list row is often the better answer when scanning matters more than presence.
terms.example: A term-of-the-day card with a heading, a one-line definition and a category, tappable as a single unit.
terms.misuse: Nested cards inside cards remove the grouping signal entirely, because everything is inside a boundary.

terms.shortDef: Participants group content labels to reveal their mental model.
terms.longDef: Each item of content is a card; participants sort them into piles that make sense to them. In an open sort they name the piles themselves, which tells you their vocabulary; in a closed sort you supply the categories and learn whether your structure holds. It informs navigation but does not design it for you.
terms.example: Sorting 60 help-article titles shows that customers group by "my money" and "my account", not by the company's internal departments.
terms.misuse: Card sorting reveals grouping, tree testing checks findability. Running only a sort leaves you guessing whether the result works.

terms.shortDef: The documented expectations for each level of a role.
terms.longDef: A ladder describes craft, scope, autonomy and influence at each level, and usually splits into individual contributor and management tracks past mid-level. Its value is making promotion criteria legible rather than political. Ladders that describe only craft tend to promote people into management as the only way to grow.
terms.example: A senior level defined by leading a project end to end, a staff level by influencing several teams' direction.

terms.shortDef: A rotating set of panels shown one or a few at a time.
terms.longDef: Carousels promise several messages in one slot and usually deliver one: engagement drops sharply after the first panel. They work better as manually scrolled lists of peers — related products, photos — than as auto-rotating hero banners. Auto-advance is a particular problem for anyone who reads slowly or relies on a screen reader.
terms.example: A horizontally scrolling row of related items, with the next one partly visible, and no automatic movement.
terms.misuse: Auto-rotating banners are the canonical example: they move away mid-read and are widely ignored as adverts.

terms.shortDef: A written account of one project, from problem to outcome.
terms.longDef: A strong case study states the problem and constraints, shows the options considered and why one was chosen, names the evidence, and reports what happened including what did not work. Length is not the point — a reviewer usually gives it a few minutes. Confidentiality can be handled by describing the reasoning without exposing the numbers.
terms.example: "Support contacts about delivery fell by a fifth; the second change we shipped had no effect and we reverted it."

terms.shortDef: Short-term backlash to a change, regardless of its quality.
terms.longDef: Existing users have built muscle memory, and any change taxes it. Complaints and dipped metrics in the first weeks after a release reflect the transition as much as the design. The mistake is either dismissing all feedback as change aversion or rolling back before the curve settles.
terms.example: A navigation move produces a spike in support tickets that halves each week for a month.
terms.misuse: Used as a shield against real criticism. If the metric never recovers, it was not change aversion.

terms.shortDef: Too many options can stop people choosing at all.
terms.longDef: Beyond a certain point, additional options reduce the likelihood of any decision and lower satisfaction with the one made. The effect depends on how comparable the options are and how much the person knows about the domain. Good defaults, filtering and recommended picks restore the ability to decide without removing the range.
terms.example: A menu of forty plans with one marked "most popular" converts better than the same forty presented flat.
terms.misuse: Not a law that fewer is always better. Experts in a domain often want the full range visible.

terms.shortDef: Grouping information into units that are easier to hold.
terms.longDef: Breaking a long string or list into meaningful groups lets working memory treat each group as one item. It applies to numbers, to form sections and to navigation. The grouping has to match how people think about the content, or it adds a structure they then have to decode.
terms.example: Sort codes shown as 20-30-40 are read back correctly far more often than 203040.

terms.shortDef: The rate at which users or customers stop using a product.
terms.longDef: Churn is retention's mirror, usually measured against subscribers or accounts over a period. Voluntary churn — people choosing to leave — is a product signal, while involuntary churn from expired cards is an operations problem with a design fix. The most informative research is with people who have just left, and it is the least often done.
terms.example: Splitting 6% monthly churn reveals a third of it is failed payments, not dissatisfaction.

terms.shortDef: Designing for differences in memory, attention and processing.
terms.longDef: It covers people with learning disabilities, ADHD, autism, brain injury and age-related change — and everyone under stress or distraction. The practical measures are plain language, consistent patterns, generous time limits, undo instead of confirmation, and never requiring information to be held in memory across steps. It is the least automated and most impactful area of accessibility.
terms.example: Showing the entered address on the confirmation step rather than asking the user to remember what they typed.

terms.shortDef: The mental effort an interface demands to be used.
terms.longDef: Load comes from three places: the inherent difficulty of the task, effort wasted on the interface itself, and effort spent actually learning. Design work is mostly about removing the second kind — unclear labels, remembered values, unnecessary decisions — so the available attention goes to the real task. It is finite and shared with whatever else the person is doing.
terms.example: Showing the delivery address on the payment step removes the need to remember what was entered two screens ago.
terms.misuse: "Reduce cognitive load" is not the same as "hide things". Hiding a needed control usually increases it.

terms.shortDef: Stepping through a task asking what a first-time user would do.
terms.longDef: At each step the reviewers ask whether the user would know what to do, whether they would see the control, and whether they would understand that their action worked. It is specifically aimed at learnability, which makes it well suited to onboarding and rarely used features. Like any expert method, it produces hypotheses rather than findings.
terms.example: Walking the two-factor setup step by step exposes that nothing on screen explains where the code will arrive.

terms.shortDef: Comparing groups defined by when they joined or what they did.
terms.longDef: Grouping users by signup month, acquisition channel or first action lets you see whether behaviour is genuinely changing, rather than being masked by new arrivals. It is what turns a flat aggregate line into an actual finding. It is also the honest way to judge whether a change helped, since only later cohorts experienced it.
terms.example: Overall retention looks flat, but each new monthly cohort retains better than the last — growth was hiding the improvement.

terms.shortDef: The restricted set of colours a product is built from.
terms.longDef: A working palette is usually a neutral ramp, one accent for interaction, and a small set of status colours — far fewer than teams expect. Deriving related hues from a single accent keeps a large system coherent where twelve unrelated colours would not. Every pair that can appear together needs its contrast checked, in both themes.
terms.example: Twelve category tints generated by rotating one accent's hue, so they read as a family rather than a rainbow.
terms.misuse: Colour must never be the only carrier of meaning; anything a colour says must also be said in text or shape.

terms.shortDef: Reduced ability to distinguish certain colours.
terms.longDef: Around one in twelve men and one in two hundred women have some form, most commonly difficulty separating red from green. The design consequence is simple and absolute: never let colour be the only thing carrying meaning. Add text, shape, position or pattern alongside it.
terms.example: A status list that pairs each colour with a written label, so red and green are not the only difference.
terms.misuse: Checking contrast ratios does not cover this. Two colours can pass contrast and still be indistinguishable to some viewers.

terms.shortDef: Studying alternatives to understand conventions and gaps.
terms.longDef: A useful analysis compares how competitors solve specific tasks, not how many features they list. It establishes what users already expect, which is what Jakob's Law makes expensive to ignore. Include indirect alternatives, since the real competitor is often a spreadsheet or a group chat.
terms.example: Walking the signup flow of five rivals and recording where each asks for a card, and how they say it.
terms.misuse: Copying a competitor's pattern assumes they tested it. Many did not, and you inherit their mistake.

terms.shortDef: A reusable interface part with defined variants and states.
terms.longDef: A component packages appearance and behaviour together, including its focus, hover, disabled, loading and error states. Defining it once means fixing an accessibility bug once. The design skill is choosing the right level of abstraction — too specific and nothing reuses it, too general and every use needs configuration.
terms.example: A single text field component handling label, hint, error, disabled and character count, used across forty forms.

terms.shortDef: Testing an idea's value before building the interface.
terms.longDef: Participants react to a description, storyboard or rough sketch to establish whether the idea is understood and wanted. It answers "should this exist" rather than "does this work". Keep the stimulus deliberately rough, or feedback drifts to visual details.
terms.example: Showing three one-page service concepts and asking which one participants would sign up for tomorrow, and why.
terms.misuse: Stated interest is weak evidence. Ask what people have already done about the problem instead of whether they would use this.

terms.shortDef: The plausible range around a measured number.
terms.longDef: A single measured figure is an estimate; the interval shows how much it could move if you measured again. Narrow intervals come from large samples and consistent behaviour. Reporting the interval alongside the number stops teams treating an estimate as a fact.
terms.example: "Task success was 72% (95% CI: 58–84%)" is honest; "task success was 72%" from eight participants is not.

terms.shortDef: Noticing the evidence that fits what you already believe.
terms.longDef: Teams unconsciously weight the sessions that supported the plan and explain away the ones that did not. It shows up in which clips get shown to stakeholders and which quotes make the deck. Pre-registering what you expect, and asking what would change your mind, is the practical defence.
terms.example: Three participants struggle with the new flow and the readout leads with the two who liked it.

terms.shortDef: Freely given, informed agreement to something specific.
terms.longDef: Valid consent requires a real choice, plain language, granularity by purpose, and the same ease of withdrawal as of giving. Pre-ticked boxes, bundled permissions and refusal paths hidden behind extra clicks all fail that bar, and increasingly fail regulation too. Asking at the moment the permission is needed, with a reason, converts better than asking up front.
terms.example: Requesting notification permission when the user turns on a reminder, explaining what will be sent, and how to stop it.
terms.misuse: Continuing to use the product is not consent. Neither is a banner whose only visible button is "Accept all".

terms.shortDef: The same thing looks and behaves the same way everywhere.
terms.longDef: Internal consistency means a pattern works identically across your own product; external consistency means it matches the platform and the wider convention. Both let learning transfer, which is why a design system is worth its overhead. Consistency loses to clarity when a situation genuinely differs — but the bar for declaring that is high.
terms.example: A destructive action that is always the rightmost button, always red-labelled and always confirmed, in every flow.
terms.misuse: Consistency is not uniformity. Forcing one component to serve two different jobs makes both worse.

terms.shortDef: A limit built in so the wrong action is impossible.
terms.longDef: Constraints prevent errors rather than reporting them: a date picker that cannot offer the 30th of February, a plug that only fits one way. They can be physical, logical, semantic or cultural. Well-placed constraints remove whole classes of error message from the product.
terms.example: Disabling past dates in a booking calendar stops the error before it happens rather than validating it afterwards.
terms.misuse: Disabling a control without explaining why is a constraint that creates confusion. Say what would make it available.

terms.shortDef: Deciding what to say, in what order, in what words.
terms.longDef: Content design treats language as part of the interface rather than a layer applied at the end, covering labels, error messages, empty states and the structure of the information itself. It often removes a screen rather than filling one. Done well it is the cheapest usability improvement available.
terms.example: Replacing "Submission unsuccessful" with "We could not take that card — check the expiry date" halves calls to support.
terms.misuse: Not the same as copywriting. Content design answers what the user needs to know; copywriting persuades.

terms.shortDef: Interviewing people while they work in their own environment.
terms.longDef: The researcher visits the place the work actually happens and watches it unfold, asking questions in the moment. It surfaces the workarounds, sticky notes and second monitors that never come up in a conference-room interview. The classic framing is master and apprentice: the participant leads, you learn.
terms.example: Sitting beside a pharmacy technician for a shift reveals they keep a handwritten list of drug codes because the system's search is too slow.
terms.misuse: Often confused with an ethnographic study. Contextual inquiry is a focused few hours around specific work; ethnography is a broader, longer immersion.

terms.shortDef: The difference in luminance between two colours.
terms.longDef: Expressed as a ratio, contrast determines whether text can be read and whether a control can be seen. WCAG 2.2 asks for at least 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text, and 3:1 for interface components and focus indicators. It is also a design tool: hierarchy is largely built from controlled differences in contrast.
terms.example: Muted grey body text on a white background must reach 4.5:1, which rules out most light greys designers reach for first.
terms.misuse: Contrast ratio is about luminance, not hue. Two colours can be very different and still fail.

terms.shortDef: A shared expectation about how something works.
terms.longDef: Conventions are learned from the wider ecosystem: a logo returns home, a magnifying glass means search, a red badge means unread. They are not laws, but breaking one spends attention that could have gone on your actual product. Conventions also differ by platform, which is why an iOS pattern transplanted to Android often feels wrong.
terms.example: Placing the primary action on the right on iOS and following the platform's own ordering on Android.

terms.shortDef: An interface where the main interaction is exchanging messages.
terms.longDef: Chat is flexible and unusually undiscoverable: a blank field advertises nothing about what the system can do. The strongest designs pair it with visible affordances — suggested prompts, structured results, controls embedded in replies. Chat suits open-ended requests and is a poor replacement for a form or a list.
terms.example: An assistant offering three starting questions and returning a filterable list rather than a paragraph.
terms.misuse: Replacing a working form with a chatbot usually adds turns to a task that took one screen.

terms.shortDef: The share of people who complete a defined goal.
terms.longDef: Conversion needs a stated denominator to mean anything — of visitors, of sessions, of people who reached step two. Rates move with traffic mix as much as with design, so a change in marketing can look like a design win. Always report the definition alongside the number.
terms.example: "4.2% of first-time visitors completed checkout" is interpretable; "4.2% conversion" is not.
terms.misuse: Comparing conversion rates across periods with different traffic sources compares audiences, not designs.

terms.shortDef: Google's three field metrics for loading, responsiveness and stability.
terms.longDef: Largest Contentful Paint measures when the main content appears, Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness to input, and Cumulative Layout Shift measures unexpected movement. They are collected from real users rather than lab runs, and they influence search ranking. For designers, CLS is the most directly controllable — it is usually caused by images and fonts without reserved space.
terms.example: Reserving the exact height of a hero image removes the shift that pushes the headline down as it loads.

terms.shortDef: Sketching eight ideas in eight minutes, one per fold.
terms.longDef: A sheet folded into eight panels, one minute per panel, forces quantity past the point where the obvious answers run out. The constraint is the method: with more time people polish their first idea instead of finding a fifth. Output is deliberately rough and mostly discarded.
terms.example: Six people produce 48 sketches in eight minutes; three genuinely new directions come from panels six to eight.

terms.shortDef: One codebase producing apps for several operating systems.
terms.longDef: Frameworks such as React Native and Flutter share most logic and interface code across iOS and Android, trading some platform fidelity for speed of delivery. The design consequence is deciding where to follow each platform's conventions and where a single shared pattern is acceptable. Navigation, back behaviour, typography and system gestures are where the difference is felt most.
terms.example: One component library rendering a shared design, with platform-specific back behaviour and system fonts respected.
terms.misuse: Cross-platform does not mean identical. Shipping an iOS interface unchanged to Android reads as a port, not an app.

terms.shortDef: How much effort a task felt like it took.
terms.longDef: Users rate agreement with a statement such as "the company made it easy to handle my issue". Effort predicts loyalty better than delight does, particularly in service interactions, because reducing friction retains people more reliably than exceeding expectations. It is asked immediately after the task, while the effort is remembered accurately.
terms.example: Asking "how easy was it to change your delivery date?" right after the change, not in a monthly survey.

terms.shortDef: A direct rating of satisfaction with a specific experience.
terms.longDef: CSAT asks how satisfied someone was, usually on a five-point scale, immediately after an interaction. Because it is tied to a moment it is far more actionable than a relationship-level score. Response bias is strong — the delighted and the furious answer, the indifferent do not.
terms.example: A one-question rating after a support chat, reported per agent, per topic and per channel.

terms.shortDef: A theme with light content on dark surfaces.
terms.longDef: Dark mode is not an inversion: pure white on pure black causes halation and is uncomfortable for many people, so both ends are usually pulled in. Shadows stop working, saturated colours look more intense, and every contrast pair needs re-checking. Following the system setting by default is the expected behaviour, with an override available.
terms.example: Body text at #EEEFF3 on a #101116 surface, with the accent lightened so it still passes contrast.
terms.misuse: Dark mode is not universally more accessible. Some people with astigmatism read light-on-dark considerably more slowly.

terms.shortDef: An interface designed to trick people into acting against their interests.
terms.longDef: Deceptive patterns include hiding the cancel path, pre-ticked consent, fake scarcity, confirmshaming and making the unsubscribe route deliberately long. They convert measurably in the short term and are increasingly illegal, most explicitly under EU and UK consumer rules. The reliable test is whether you would explain the design to the user honestly.
terms.example: A subscription that takes one tap to start and a phone call during business hours to cancel.
terms.misuse: Not every persuasive design is deceptive. The line is whether the user's understanding is being deliberately impaired.

terms.shortDef: A calendar control for choosing dates.
terms.longDef: Pickers help when the day of the week or availability matters, and hinder when the date is simply known — a birth date is faster typed than found in a calendar twelve taps back. The strongest pattern offers both: a typed field that accepts several formats, with a calendar available. Ranges need the two ends to remain visible and editable.
terms.example: A hotel booking shows a calendar with unavailable nights disabled; a passport form offers three simple fields instead.
terms.misuse: Forcing a calendar for distant dates is the classic version of this mistake, most visibly on date-of-birth fields.

terms.shortDef: Daily actives over monthly actives, as a stickiness ratio.
terms.longDef: The ratio estimates how many days a month a typical user shows up. It suits products meant to be used daily and misleads badly for those with a natural weekly or seasonal rhythm. "Active" has to be defined as something meaningful — an app open is not use.
terms.example: A ratio of 0.5 means the average monthly user opens the product about fifteen days a month.
terms.misuse: Chasing the ratio for a product people should only need occasionally optimises for a behaviour nobody wants.

terms.shortDef: A link that opens a specific screen inside an app.
terms.longDef: Deep links let a search result, an email or a shared message land someone exactly where they need to be rather than on a home screen. They require the destination to be reachable from a cold start, with the right back behaviour when there is no history. Handling the case where the app is not installed is part of the design.
terms.example: Tapping a shared definition opens that term directly, with a back action that goes to search rather than out of the app.

terms.shortDef: How much information is packed into a given area.
terms.longDef: High density suits expert tools where scanning and comparison matter more than comfort; low density suits occasional use and small screens. It is a deliberate setting, not a side effect, and some products offer it as a user preference. Density must never be achieved by shrinking touch targets or contrast.
terms.example: A dictionary list showing term and one line of definition per row, so scanning beats tapping into each entry.

terms.shortDef: Structured feedback on work against its stated goals.
terms.longDef: A critique judges the work against the problem it set out to solve, not against the reviewer's taste. It works when the presenter states the goal and the specific question they want answered, and when feedback describes an observed effect rather than prescribing a fix. Without that structure it becomes a series of preferences.
terms.example: "The primary action reads as secondary to me because it is quieter than the cancel link" — an observation, not an instruction.
terms.misuse: "I don't like the blue" is not critique. Feedback without a reason cannot be acted on or argued with.

terms.shortDef: Accumulated shortcuts that make the experience inconsistent.
terms.longDef: Every deadline-driven exception — a one-off component, an unhandled state, a pattern used two ways — is borrowed time repaid with interest in confusion and rework. Like technical debt it is sometimes worth taking deliberately, provided it is recorded. Unrecorded, it is simply decay.
terms.example: Four different date pickers across one product, each with its own bugs and its own accessibility problems.

terms.shortDef: Weighing the effects of a design on the people subject to it.
terms.longDef: Ethical questions in design usually concern consent, honesty, autonomy, data and who is excluded or harmed. They arise most sharply where the business's interest and the user's diverge, which is exactly where designers have leverage. The practical version is a habit: ask who could be harmed, and whether you would explain the design honestly to the person affected.
terms.example: Declining to add a countdown timer that creates false urgency, and proposing an honest stock indicator instead.

terms.shortDef: Someone accountable for a design team rather than for the designs.
terms.longDef: The job is hiring, growing people, setting quality expectations, protecting focus and representing design outside the team. Craft judgement is still needed, but exercised through critique and standards rather than by doing the work. The common failure is a manager who keeps designing and leaves the team unmanaged.
terms.example: Running weekly critique, setting the quality bar for accessibility, and negotiating research time with product leadership.

terms.shortDef: How deeply design practice is embedded in an organisation.
terms.longDef: Low maturity treats design as a service that styles decisions already made; high maturity involves design in framing problems and measures experience alongside commercial results. It shows in when designers are consulted, whether research budget exists, and whether accessibility is a requirement or a request. Knowing where an organisation sits is the most useful thing a candidate can establish in an interview.
terms.example: Being asked to "make this screen nicer" a week before launch is a reliable indicator of low maturity.

terms.shortDef: A reusable solution to a recurring interface problem.
terms.longDef: A pattern describes the problem, the context it applies in, and the shape of the solution — search-as-you-type, the empty state, the confirmation dialog. It is more abstract than a component: one pattern may be built from several components, or realised differently on each platform. Patterns document why, components deliver what.
terms.example: The "select from recent items" pattern appears as a dropdown on desktop and a bottom sheet on mobile.

terms.shortDef: A checkpoint where stakeholders assess work before it proceeds.
terms.longDef: Unlike critique, a review exists to make a decision: proceed, change, or stop. It needs the decision-maker present, the criteria known in advance and the work at a fidelity that matches the question. Reviews held too late produce expensive changes and resentful teams.
terms.example: A pre-build review confirms the flow, the states and the edge cases before engineering estimates the work.
terms.misuse: Reviews are not for gathering opinions from everyone available. Invite people who own a decision or a constraint.

terms.shortDef: A structured week to go from problem to tested prototype.
terms.longDef: Five days: understand the problem, sketch, decide, build a realistic prototype, then test with five people. Its value is the forcing function — a decision and evidence inside a week, with the right people in one room. It is expensive in senior time and works badly on problems that are not yet well framed.
terms.example: A team spends Monday to Thursday on a booking-flow prototype and interviews five customers on Friday morning.
terms.misuse: A design sprint is not an agile sprint. One is a five-day workshop format, the other a recurring delivery cadence.

terms.shortDef: Shared components, tokens and rules used to build a product.
terms.longDef: A design system pairs documented principles and patterns with the actual code and design components teams build from, so consistency is the default rather than an act of discipline. Its hard parts are governance and adoption, not the components. An unmaintained system is worse than none, because teams work around it and lose trust in it.
terms.example: One Button component with defined variants, states and accessibility behaviour, used by every squad and versioned like any dependency.
terms.misuse: A file of Figma components is not a design system unless the built product actually consumes the equivalent code.

terms.shortDef: Someone who designs and builds, usually in a design system.
terms.longDef: They live between the two disciplines: prototyping in code, maintaining component libraries, and making sure what is designed can be built consistently. The role is most valuable where a design system exists, because that is where design decisions become code. It requires genuine competence in both, which is why the role is scarce.
terms.example: Building the production Button component and its documentation from the design team's token definitions.

terms.shortDef: A problem-solving approach that starts from people's needs.
terms.longDef: Usually taught as empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test, repeated. Its contribution was making user-centred method legible to people outside design, especially executives. It is criticised for reducing craft to workshops, and it works best as a shared vocabulary rather than as the whole of a design practice.
terms.example: A hospital team runs the five stages over six weeks to redesign discharge paperwork, testing three paper prototypes with patients.
terms.misuse: Running a sticky-note workshop is not design thinking. Without research and iteration it is just a meeting.

terms.shortDef: A named value for a design decision, used everywhere it applies.
terms.longDef: Tokens store decisions — a colour, a spacing step, a radius, a duration — as names rather than raw values, so the decision has one home. Semantic names such as `surface-raised` outlive literal ones such as `grey-100`, because the meaning survives a rebrand. They are what makes theming and dark mode a configuration change rather than a rewrite.
terms.example: `color.text.muted` resolves to one grey in light mode and a different one in dark, with no component knowing either value.
terms.misuse: Naming a token after its value defeats the purpose. `blue-500` cannot be changed to green without lying.

terms.shortDef: The systems that let a design team work at scale.
terms.longDef: DesignOps covers tooling, file structure, onboarding, rituals, hiring pipelines and the health of the design system — the work that is nobody's project but everybody's problem. It becomes necessary somewhere around ten designers, when coordination cost starts to exceed craft cost. The measure of success is designers spending more time designing.
terms.example: Standardising component libraries and file naming across six squads cuts the time to start a new project from days to hours.

terms.shortDef: Measuring the impression a design's look and tone creates.
terms.longDef: Participants pick words from a fixed list — trustworthy, cluttered, dated, playful — to describe a design, and then explain their choices. Using a supplied vocabulary avoids the vagueness of "I like it". It measures brand perception rather than usability.
terms.example: A fintech redesign is described as "serious" and "secure" by most participants, and "cold" by half of them.

terms.shortDef: How many physical pixels make up one logical design unit.
terms.longDef: Designs are specified in logical units — points on iOS, density-independent pixels on Android, CSS pixels on the web — and the device multiplies them by its ratio. A 44pt target is the same physical size on a 2x and a 3x screen. Raster assets need exporting at each multiple; vector assets avoid the problem.
terms.example: A 24pt icon exported at 48px and 72px for 2x and 3x displays, or shipped once as a vector.
terms.misuse: Designing in physical pixels leads to interfaces that shrink on higher-density screens.

terms.shortDef: Participants log their own experiences over days or weeks.
terms.longDef: Participants record entries as things happen, usually prompted by a notification or a scheduled reminder. It captures behaviour that a single session cannot reach: how a habit forms, when frustration builds, what people do between sessions. Compliance is the hard part, so entries need to take under a minute.
terms.example: Thirty commuters photograph their ticket screen every time they board for two weeks, revealing that glare is the real barrier, not the interface.

terms.shortDef: Whether people notice a feature exists at all.
terms.longDef: A feature nobody finds is a feature nobody has. Discoverability is driven by signifiers, by placement in the flow where the need arises, and by whether the interface hints that more is available. Hidden gestures are the classic failure — powerful for those who know, invisible to everyone else.
terms.example: Pull-to-refresh is undiscoverable on its own, which is why apps that rely on it also provide a visible refresh control.
terms.misuse: Not the same as findability. People can fail to find a page they knew about, and fail to discover a feature they did not.

terms.shortDef: Opening up options, then deliberately narrowing them down.
terms.longDef: Divergence generates possibilities without judging them; convergence evaluates and commits. Mixing the two in one conversation is what makes design meetings unproductive, because critique kills generation. Naming which mode the room is in is a small intervention with a large effect.
terms.example: A workshop where the first hour has an explicit no-critique rule and the second hour is nothing but critique.

terms.shortDef: Below about 400ms response, attention holds and productivity rises.
terms.longDef: When a system responds faster than roughly four hundred milliseconds, people stay in the loop rather than waiting on it, and their pace increases sharply. Above it, attention wanders and the session slows disproportionately. It is why perceived performance work — optimistic updates, skeletons, prefetching — pays back more than it costs.
terms.example: Search that filters as you type keeps you engaged; the same search behind a submit button and a two-second wait does not.
terms.misuse: Adding a spinner does not meet the threshold. It acknowledges the wait rather than removing it.

terms.shortDef: A four-stage model alternating between widening and narrowing.
terms.longDef: Discover and Develop are divergent, opening up problems and then solutions; Define and Deliver are convergent, committing to one problem and then one answer. Its value is making explicit that you should not narrow while you are still exploring. Its weakness is that real projects loop rather than march through it once.
terms.example: A team spends three weeks on research and opportunity mapping before writing a single problem statement to design against.
terms.misuse: Not a project plan. Treating the four stages as sequential phases with sign-off gates recreates waterfall with nicer diagrams.

terms.shortDef: Moving something by picking it up and releasing it elsewhere.
terms.longDef: Direct manipulation is intuitive for reordering and for spatial arrangement, and it demands clear signals: what can be dragged, where it can go, and what happened. It is hard for people with motor impairments and impossible with a screen reader unless a keyboard equivalent exists. Always provide one.
terms.example: A reorderable list where items can also be moved with a "move up" control and with keyboard arrows when focused.
terms.misuse: Drag as the only way to perform an action is an accessibility failure, and one that WCAG 2.2 addresses directly.

terms.shortDef: A control that hides a list of options until opened.
terms.longDef: Dropdowns save space at the cost of hiding the options, which makes them poor for short lists and for anything people need to compare. Under about six options, radio buttons or segmented controls are faster and clearer. Above about twenty, add search rather than scrolling.
terms.example: Two options — monthly or yearly — belong as visible radio buttons, not behind a select.
terms.misuse: Using a dropdown for a two-item choice adds two interactions to a decision that could have taken none.

terms.shortDef: Respecting the text size the user set at system level.
terms.longDef: Many people run their phone at larger text permanently, and layouts must survive it — up to 200% is the usual requirement. That means no fixed heights on text containers, no truncation of essential content, and rows that stack when they run out of width. Testing at the largest setting exposes problems no other test does.
terms.example: A list row that shows term and definition side by side at default size and stacks them at 200%.
terms.misuse: Disabling font scaling to protect a layout is a defect, not a solution — it overrides a setting the user chose deliberately.

terms.shortDef: Typographic and language choices that reduce reading effort.
terms.longDef: The evidence supports generous line spacing, left-aligned unjustified text, short lines, clear everyday typefaces and reduced glare from pure white backgrounds. Support for specialist dyslexia typefaces is weak; ordinary well-set text tends to perform as well or better. Letting users adjust spacing and colour themselves is the most reliable measure.
terms.example: Left-aligned body text at 1.55 line height on an off-white surface, with no justified columns.
terms.misuse: Installing a "dyslexia font" is not a substitute for good typesetting, and research has not shown it to help.

terms.shortDef: A rare input or state that breaks the intended design.
terms.longDef: Long names, zero results, no network, a hundred items, a negative balance, someone in crisis — these are where a design either holds or falls apart. Many so-called edge cases are common for someone, which is why some teams call them stress cases instead. Designing them is not optional work left for engineering.
terms.example: A profile card designed for "Ada Lovelace" that breaks entirely on a 40-character name with no spaces.
terms.misuse: Labelling something an edge case is often a way of deciding not to design it. Check how many people it actually affects.

terms.shortDef: How much effort a task takes once someone knows how.
terms.longDef: One of usability's core dimensions alongside learnability, memorability, errors and satisfaction. It is measured in time, steps or interactions for experienced users, which makes it distinct from how easy something is the first time. Optimising for first-time ease can quietly make daily use slower, which is the classic tension in expert tools.
terms.example: A keyboard shortcut cuts a five-step routine task to one, while the visible menu path stays for newcomers.

terms.shortDef: The apparent layering of surfaces, usually shown by shadow.
terms.longDef: Elevation communicates which surface is on top and therefore which is currently in play — a sheet over a page, a menu over content. Shadow is one way to show it; in dark themes a lighter surface colour usually reads better than a shadow, which is invisible against black. Whatever the technique, layers should be a small defined set.
terms.example: A dialog raised over a dimmed page, and a dark-mode version that lightens the surface instead of adding a shadow.

terms.shortDef: A grid capturing what a user says, thinks, does and feels.
terms.longDef: Research observations are sorted into quadrants to make the gap between stated and actual behaviour visible — what someone says versus what they do is often the finding. It is a synthesis tool, best filled from transcripts rather than from imagination. Its output usually feeds a persona or a journey map.
terms.example: A participant says the process is fine, but the "does" quadrant records three attempts and a call to support.

terms.shortDef: What a screen shows when there is nothing to show.
terms.longDef: Empty states are the first thing new users see and the last thing designed. A good one explains why the space is empty, what will fill it, and offers the action that starts. There are several kinds — first use, no results, everything cleared — and they need different words.
terms.example: "Nothing saved yet. Save a term from its page and it lands here." with a button to find one.
terms.misuse: An illustration with no action is decoration. The empty state's job is to move the person forward.

terms.shortDef: How much people use a product, however you define use.
terms.longDef: Engagement is only meaningful once you say which action counts and why it indicates value. More time in a product can mean it is compelling or that it is confusing, and the two are indistinguishable in the number alone. For tools whose value is speed, falling engagement time is a success.
terms.example: For a lookup tool, more sessions and shorter ones is the good direction, not more minutes per session.
terms.misuse: Optimising engagement without asking what the user came for is how products end up designed against their users.

terms.shortDef: Designing so the mistake cannot happen in the first place.
terms.longDef: Better than a good error message is a design where the error is impossible or is caught before it costs anything. Constraints, sensible defaults, confirmation for irreversible actions and forgiving input formats all do this. Slips need protection; genuine mistakes need better understanding upstream.
terms.example: Asking "delete 42 files?" before an irreversible action, and offering undo for a reversible one.
terms.misuse: A confirmation dialog on every action trains people to dismiss them, which removes the protection you were buying.

terms.shortDef: How often people take a wrong action during a task.
terms.longDef: Errors are counted per task or per attempt, usually split into slips, where the intention was right, and mistakes, where the plan was wrong. High error rates on a recoverable step matter less than low rates on an irreversible one. Categorising errors points at the fix better than the total does.
terms.example: Seven of twenty participants type the date in the wrong format, all of them in the field with no placeholder.

terms.shortDef: What the interface shows when something has gone wrong.
terms.longDef: A usable error says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's language and next to the thing that caused it. It should never blame the user or expose an internal code alone. Recoverable errors keep the user's input intact — losing a filled form to a validation error is its own failure.
terms.example: "That card expired in 2024. Check the expiry date or use another card", shown beside the field, with the number preserved.
terms.misuse: "An error occurred" tells the user nothing they did not already know and offers no way forward.

terms.shortDef: Research that judges a design you have already made.
terms.longDef: Evaluative studies test something concrete — a prototype, a live flow, a competitor — against tasks or criteria. Formative evaluation runs during design to find problems while they are cheap to fix; summative evaluation measures the finished thing to establish a benchmark. Both need a design to react to.
terms.example: Testing a checkout prototype with eight people mid-sprint is formative; measuring success rate on the shipped version is summative.

terms.shortDef: Making it clear why a system produced a particular output.
terms.longDef: Users need enough of the reasoning to decide whether to trust a result: which sources were used, which signals mattered, how confident the system is. Full technical interpretability is rarely available, so interface-level explanation — provenance, confidence and the ability to inspect inputs — carries the weight. In several regulated domains it is a legal requirement.
terms.example: A recommendation labelled "because you saved three accessibility terms", with a control to change that signal.

terms.shortDef: Interfaces placed in or over three-dimensional space.
terms.longDef: Augmented reality overlays content on the world, virtual reality replaces it, and the umbrella term covers both. Design gains depth, gaze, physical scale and comfort as materials and constraints: content too close causes strain, and unanchored movement causes nausea. Text remains hard, so information density has to fall sharply compared with a screen.
terms.example: Anchoring a label to a real object so it stays put as the viewer moves, rather than floating fixed in view.

terms.shortDef: Recording where and how long people look on screen.
terms.longDef: Hardware or webcam software records gaze position, producing fixation maps and scan paths. It answers whether something was seen at all, which self-report cannot. It is expensive, needs careful calibration, and looking at something is not the same as understanding it.
terms.example: Gaze maps show that a promotional banner in the top right is skipped entirely, consistent with banner blindness.
terms.misuse: A heat map from clicks or scrolling is not eye tracking, though the visual output looks similar.

terms.shortDef: Accumulated additions that make a product harder to use.
terms.longDef: Each feature seems justified alone, and together they crowd the interface, slow the product and raise the cost of every future change. It happens because adding is easier to approve than removing, and because features are visible while complexity is not. The counterweight is an explicit removal practice and a willingness to say no with a reason.
terms.example: A settings screen that has grown to forty toggles, half of which fewer than one percent of users have ever changed.
terms.misuse: Scope creep is about a project's boundaries growing during delivery; feature creep is about a product accumulating over releases.

terms.shortDef: A switch that turns a feature on for some users without redeploying.
terms.longDef: Flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature, which makes gradual rollouts, experiments and instant rollbacks possible. They are the mechanism behind most A/B tests. They also accumulate: an old flag left in place is a permanent branch in the product's behaviour that nobody remembers.
terms.example: Releasing a new checkout to 5% of traffic, watching error rates for a day, then widening it.

terms.shortDef: Telling the user what just happened and what the system is doing.
terms.longDef: Every action needs an acknowledgement, in a form and at a speed that matches the action's weight. Immediate and small for a tap, explicit and persistent for a payment. Silence is read as failure, which is why people press submit twice.
terms.example: A button that switches to "Saving…" and then "Saved" prevents the double-submit that a silent button invites.
terms.misuse: A spinner is not feedback about outcome, only about activity. It still has to end in a result.

terms.shortDef: How closely an artefact resembles the finished product.
terms.longDef: Fidelity varies independently along several axes: visual polish, content realism, and interactivity. A grey prototype with real copy and working navigation is low fidelity visually and high fidelity functionally. Choosing fidelity is choosing what kind of feedback you will get, so match it to the question you are asking.
terms.example: Testing whether people understand a term needs real content at low visual fidelity; testing legibility needs the opposite.
terms.misuse: High fidelity is not the same as finished. A polished prototype invites polish feedback whether or not you wanted it.

terms.shortDef: Research conducted where people live or work, not in a lab.
terms.longDef: Rather than bringing people to you, you go to them and observe behaviour in its real setting, with its real interruptions and constraints. It is the best way to discover problems nobody thought to report. It is also expensive and hard to schedule, so teams usually run a handful of visits and treat them as directional.
terms.example: Visiting three warehouses shows that scanners are used one-handed while holding a box, which kills a two-thumb interface.

terms.shortDef: The eye separates a subject from its background automatically.
terms.longDef: Perception assigns one region as the object of attention and the rest as backdrop, using contrast, size and overlap to decide. Modals, dropdowns and focused states all depend on the separation being unmistakable. When figure and ground are too close in value, the interface feels flat and nothing seems clickable.
terms.example: A dialog over a dimmed page reads instantly as the thing to deal with; the same dialog with no scrim competes with the content.

terms.shortDef: Narrowing a set of results by attribute.
terms.longDef: Filters remove items that do not match, and work best when the applied filters stay visible, the result count updates immediately, and combinations that would return nothing are disabled or flagged. They depend entirely on the quality of the underlying metadata. Sorting reorders the same set and should never be confused with filtering.
terms.example: Applying "in stock" and "under £50" shows both as removable chips above a live count of matching items.
terms.misuse: Filters and sorting are often merged into one menu, which leaves people unsure whether items disappeared or moved.

terms.shortDef: How easily people locate something they are looking for.
terms.longDef: Findability depends on labels matching the words people use, on structure matching their expectations, and on search covering the gaps. It is measurable: give people a target and count how many reach it and by which route. It is distinct from discoverability, which is about noticing things you were not looking for.
terms.example: Only 30% of participants find the returns policy, and half of those reach it through search rather than navigation.
terms.misuse: Adding a search box does not fix findability. Search that returns nothing for the words people actually use is worse.

terms.shortDef: Measuring where people click first when given a task.
terms.longDef: Participants see a static screen and click once. The first click is strongly predictive: people who start down the right path usually finish, and people who start wrong usually stay wrong. It is cheap enough to run on a screenshot before anything is built.
terms.example: Testing a homepage image shows most people click the hero banner rather than the "Track order" link they were asked to find.

terms.shortDef: Targets that are bigger and closer are faster to hit.
terms.longDef: The time to reach a target depends on its size and its distance from where the pointer already is. It is the reason primary actions are large, the reason screen edges are valuable, and the reason a 20-pixel close button is a bad idea on a phone. On touch devices the finger, not the cursor, sets the minimum.
terms.example: The macOS menu bar is fast because the screen edge stops the pointer — the target is effectively infinitely tall.
terms.misuse: Making a destructive button huge is Fitts's Law working against you. Speed is not always the goal.

terms.shortDef: Showing a screen briefly, then asking what people remember.
terms.longDef: A participant sees a design for about five seconds, then answers questions about what the page is for and what stood out. It measures first impressions and hierarchy, not usability. Useful for landing pages, where the whole job is communicating one thing quickly.
terms.example: After five seconds on a pricing page, most participants recall the logo and the illustration but not the price.
terms.misuse: It tests recall and clarity, not whether a flow works. A design can pass a five-second test and still fail every task.

terms.shortDef: A moderated group discussion about attitudes and reactions.
terms.longDef: Six to ten people discuss a topic while a moderator keeps the conversation moving. Groups are useful for hearing shared language, spotting disagreement and testing early concepts. They are unreliable for usability, because the loudest participant shapes the room and nobody is doing the task.
terms.example: A bank runs two groups to hear how customers actually describe overdraft charges before naming the feature.
terms.misuse: Frequently used as a substitute for usability testing. Group opinion predicts individual behaviour badly.

terms.shortDef: The visible marker showing which element the keyboard is on.
terms.longDef: Without it, keyboard users cannot tell where they are. WCAG 2.2 requires the indicator to be clearly visible against both the element and its background, with enough contrast and area. Removing the default outline without providing a better one is a well-known and serious defect.
terms.example: A two-pixel outline offset from the control, in a colour that meets 3:1 against both surfaces, in light and dark themes.
terms.misuse: Suppressing focus outlines because they look untidy makes the product unusable for anyone not using a pointer.

terms.shortDef: Moving keyboard focus deliberately when the interface changes.
terms.longDef: When a dialog opens, focus moves into it and is contained there; when it closes, focus returns to what opened it. When content is replaced, focus goes to the new content rather than being dumped at the top. Getting this wrong silently strands keyboard and screen-reader users somewhere they cannot see.
terms.example: Opening settings moves focus to its heading; closing it returns focus to the Settings button that was pressed.
terms.misuse: A focus trap is correct inside a modal and a serious bug anywhere else, where it prevents leaving a component at all.

terms.shortDef: Structuring input so people can complete it without errors.
terms.longDef: The reliable rules are few: one column, labels above fields, related fields grouped, only the questions you genuinely need, and input types that match the data. Every removed field measurably improves completion. Most form problems are content problems — people cannot tell what is being asked.
terms.example: Splitting a 22-field application into four grouped steps with a progress marker raises completion substantially.
terms.misuse: Placeholder text as a label disappears on typing and fails accessibility. Labels stay visible.

terms.shortDef: The F-shaped path eyes take across dense unformatted text.
terms.longDef: Eye-tracking shows readers scanning the first lines fully, then progressively less of each line, forming an F. It is a symptom of text that has not been structured, not a layout to design toward. The response is subheadings, front-loaded sentences and lists, which change the pattern entirely.
terms.example: A wall of paragraphs produces the F; the same content with subheadings and bold lead-ins is scanned much more evenly.
terms.misuse: It is not a template. Designing an F-shaped layout misreads a description of failure as a recommendation.

terms.shortDef: The sequence of steps toward a goal, and the loss at each.
terms.longDef: A funnel counts how many people reach each step, making the biggest drop visible. The largest fall is not always the best target — a small drop at a high-value step can be worth more. Funnels only describe the path you defined, so people who succeed by another route look like failures.
terms.example: Basket to delivery loses 12%, delivery to payment loses 41%, which points the work at the payment step.
terms.misuse: A funnel says where people leave, never why. Pair it with session replay or interviews before redesigning anything.

terms.shortDef: Models that produce new text, images, audio or code.
terms.longDef: Rather than classifying an input, generative models produce an output that did not exist before, from a prompt or another input. For designers the shift is that outputs are probabilistic: the same request can produce different results, so interfaces need to handle variation, review and correction. Designing the review step is usually more important than designing the input.
terms.example: A summary feature that generates a draft, marks it as generated, and puts it in an editor rather than publishing it.
terms.misuse: Not all AI is generative. Recommendation, search ranking and classification are long-standing uses that produce no new content.

terms.shortDef: Research done before you know what to build.
terms.longDef: Generative work explores a problem space: who these people are, what they are trying to achieve, where today's process breaks. It runs before solutions exist and its output is framing — opportunities, jobs, a map of the territory. Skipping it is how teams end up building a well-designed answer to the wrong question.
terms.example: Before designing a scheduling tool, a team shadows six clinic receptionists to learn how appointments really get booked.
terms.misuse: Not a synonym for "early". You can run evaluative research early and generative research late; the difference is whether you are exploring or judging.

terms.shortDef: An action performed by moving a finger on a touchscreen.
terms.longDef: Swipes, pinches and long presses are fast for people who know them and invisible to everyone else, because they leave no trace on screen. Treat them as accelerators layered on top of a visible control, never as the only route. Every gesture also needs an accessible equivalent.
terms.example: Swiping a row to delete, with the same delete available in the row's menu and as a screen-reader action.
terms.misuse: Hidden gestures are a frequent cause of undiscoverable features. If it is not signalled, most people never find it.

terms.shortDef: Effort increases as a visible goal gets closer.
terms.longDef: People speed up the nearer they are to finishing, which makes visible progress a powerful completion aid. Starting someone partway along — two stamps already on the loyalty card — triggers the same acceleration. The progress shown has to be real, or the trust cost outweighs the completion gain.
terms.example: A four-step checkout that marks step one complete on arrival sees fewer drop-offs than one starting at zero.

terms.shortDef: Failing partially and usefully rather than completely.
terms.longDef: When something is unavailable — the network, a font, a permission, a third-party service — the product should lose that capability and keep the rest. It requires designing the degraded state deliberately, including what the user is told. The alternative is a blank screen, which is a design decision made by omission.
terms.example: Losing connectivity disables the update check and leaves search, saved terms and revision fully working.

terms.shortDef: An underlying structure of columns and gutters for placing content.
terms.longDef: A grid gives alignment and proportion without re-deciding them per screen, and it makes responsive behaviour describable — what merges, what stacks, what disappears. It should be a servant: breaking it deliberately for one element is often what creates emphasis. A grid that nothing ever breaks tends to produce very even, very dull layouts.
terms.example: A four-column phone grid becoming twelve columns on desktop, with the reading column capped regardless.

terms.shortDef: A number watched to make sure a win is not causing harm elsewhere.
terms.longDef: Guardrails catch the damage a primary metric cannot see: complaints, unsubscribes, load time, accessibility failures, support volume. They are agreed with the success metric and given thresholds that would stop a rollout. Without them, local optimisation reliably produces global harm.
