terms.example: A conversion win is not shipped because refund requests and support contacts both rose beyond their thresholds.

terms.shortDef: Quick informal testing with whoever is nearby.
terms.longDef: You approach people in a café, a lobby or the next desk and ask for five minutes with a prototype. It catches obvious problems fast and cheaply, which makes it valuable early. It cannot support claims about your actual audience, because you did not choose who took part.
terms.example: Ten minutes in a coffee shop shows that nobody recognises the icon the team spent a week debating.
terms.misuse: Convenient participants are not representative ones. Never report a guerrilla result as a rate.

terms.shortDef: The gap between the system's state and the user's understanding of it.
terms.longDef: Norman describes two gulfs: execution, the distance between what someone wants to do and the actions available, and evaluation, the distance between what the system did and what they can tell about it. Feedback narrows the second; clear affordances and signifiers narrow the first. Most confusing interfaces are wide in one or both.
terms.example: A sync icon that spins forever leaves a wide gulf of evaluation — the user cannot tell whether their work is safe.

terms.shortDef: A model producing confident output that is simply false.
terms.longDef: Because generation optimises for plausibility, models invent citations, quotes, prices and facts in the same tone as correct ones. There is no reliable internal signal for it, so the interface has to carry the burden: cite sources, show what the answer was drawn from, and make verification cheap. Never present generated content as authoritative without a route to check it.
terms.example: A generated summary attributes a statistic to a real report that does not contain it, phrased exactly like a true citation.
terms.misuse: The word implies a perceptual error. The model is not mistaken about reality; it has no model of reality to be mistaken about.

terms.shortDef: Navigation hidden behind a three-line icon.
terms.longDef: The pattern trades discoverability for screen space: everything is available but nothing is visible. Measured against visible navigation it consistently reduces engagement with the sections inside it. It remains reasonable for genuinely secondary destinations, and unreasonable for the main ones.
terms.example: Moving "Saved" out of a drawer and into a visible tab typically increases its use several times over.
terms.misuse: Adding the word "Menu" beside the icon helps recognition but does not fix the underlying cost of hiding things.

terms.shortDef: Passing design decisions to the people who will build them.
terms.longDef: Handoff covers specs, states, behaviours, edge cases and the reasoning behind the choices — not just the visual file. It works best as a conversation running throughout the work rather than an event at the end. The word itself is contested, because teams that hand off tend to produce work that neither side owns.
terms.example: A shared page listing every state of a component, including empty, loading, error and 200-character content.
terms.misuse: A link to the design file is not a handoff. Anything not specified will be decided by whoever builds it.

terms.shortDef: Physical feedback delivered through vibration.
terms.longDef: A short tap confirms an action without requiring the user to look, which is valuable when the device is in a pocket, when someone is walking, or when vision is limited. It has to be sparing and meaningful — constant buzzing is quickly turned off. Platforms define standard intensities for selection, success and warning.
terms.example: A light tap when a flashcard flips, and a slightly heavier one when an answer is graded.
terms.misuse: Haptics as the only signal excludes people who have them disabled, and anyone using a device without them.

terms.shortDef: Headings nested in order, describing the shape of the content.
terms.longDef: Headings are the primary way screen-reader users navigate, so levels must reflect meaning rather than the size that looked right. One top-level heading per screen, with no skipped levels, produces an outline that can be scanned in seconds. It benefits sighted users too, since the same structure drives visual hierarchy.
terms.example: A term page with the headword as the page heading and Example, Related terms and Sources as second-level headings.
terms.misuse: Choosing a heading level for its font size is the most common cause of broken outlines. Style and level are separate decisions.

terms.shortDef: Five UX metric categories: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, task success.
terms.longDef: Developed at Google to give user experience a metric set beyond business numbers. Each category is turned into concrete measures through goals, signals and metrics — deciding what success means, what behaviour would show it, and what to count. Teams are advised to pick one or two categories, not all five.
terms.example: For a lookup tool: task success measured as searches that end in a term being opened, and happiness by a periodic CSAT.

terms.shortDef: A colour overlay showing where people click, move or scroll.
terms.longDef: Heatmaps show aggregate attention or activity on a page, which is useful for spotting ignored regions and unexpected clicks on non-interactive elements. They flatten different intentions into one picture and cannot distinguish a confident click from a confused one. They also break on dynamic content, where the same coordinates hold different things for different people.
terms.example: A scroll map showing 70% of visitors never reach the pricing table halfway down the page.
terms.misuse: A click heatmap is not eye tracking, though the output looks similar. It records the hand, not the eye.

terms.shortDef: Experts inspect an interface against a set of usability rules.
terms.longDef: Several evaluators independently walk the interface against a checklist such as Nielsen's ten, then merge and rate their findings by severity. It is fast, needs no participants, and catches obvious problems before spending research time. It predicts problems rather than observing them, and evaluators find things real users never hit.
terms.example: Three reviewers each list violations in a signup flow; the merged list of 27 issues is cut to nine rated severe.
terms.misuse: Not a replacement for usability testing. It is a cheap first pass that makes the testing you do more valuable.

terms.shortDef: The more choices you show, the longer the decision takes.
terms.longDef: Decision time grows with the number and complexity of the options presented. The practical response is not always fewer features but fewer things visible at once: group, prioritise and defer. It applies to considered choices, not to scanning a familiar list where people already know what they want.
terms.example: A signup screen offering three plans converts faster than one offering eleven, even when the eleven include the three.
terms.misuse: Not a mandate to strip everything back. A long alphabetical list of countries is fine, because nobody is comparing them.

terms.shortDef: A question format that turns a problem into an invitation.
terms.longDef: Phrasing an insight as "How might we…" keeps it open enough to allow several answers while staying specific enough to be useful. Too broad and it is unanswerable; too narrow and it contains the solution already. Teams usually generate many and then vote on which to work against.
terms.example: "How might we help first-time sellers price an item without research?" sits between "how might we improve selling" and "how might we add a price slider".

terms.shortDef: Keeping a person's judgement inside an automated process.
terms.longDef: The person reviews, corrects or approves before an output takes effect, which is the main safeguard against confident errors. It only works if review is genuinely possible: enough context, enough time, and no pressure to rubber-stamp. Automation bias is real — people accept a machine's suggestion more readily than a colleague's.
terms.example: Generated alt text presented pre-filled and editable, requiring a deliberate save before it is published.
terms.misuse: A confirmation button is not oversight if the reviewer cannot see what they are approving or is shown fifty an hour.

terms.shortDef: A testable statement of what you expect and why.
terms.longDef: A usable hypothesis names the change, the expected effect, the audience and the measure — and it is falsifiable. Writing it before the work stops the team from reinterpreting whatever happened as a success. It also forces the question of what result would make you revert.
terms.example: "Showing delivery cost on the product page will reduce basket abandonment for new customers by at least three points."
terms.misuse: "We think this will improve the experience" is not a hypothesis. Nothing could disprove it.

terms.shortDef: A small symbol standing for an object or an action.
terms.longDef: Only a handful of icons are universally understood — home, search, print, close — and everything else is learned or guessed. Pairing an icon with a text label removes the guessing and costs very little space. Icons still earn their place: they speed recognition for familiar users and anchor scanning.
terms.example: A bookmark icon with the word "Saved" beneath it in a tab bar, so neither has to carry the meaning alone.
terms.misuse: An unlabelled icon whose meaning is only revealed on hover is the mystery-meat problem, and it fails entirely on touch.

terms.shortDef: Deliberately generating many options before choosing one.
terms.longDef: The point is volume and range, produced under a rule that judgement is suspended until later. Working individually before sharing produces more variety than group brainstorming, which tends to converge on the first idea voiced. The output is raw material, not a decision.
terms.example: Each person sketches eight ideas in eight minutes alone, then the group posts them all up and clusters before discussing any.
terms.misuse: Ideating without a frame produces a wall of unusable ideas. Decide what question you are answering first.

terms.shortDef: Payment offered for a participant's time in a study.
terms.longDef: Incentives compensate people for time and travel, and they widen the pool beyond enthusiasts willing to help for free. Set them by session length and how hard the audience is to reach, not by what you can get away with. Under-paying quietly biases your sample toward people with time to spare.
terms.example: A 60-minute remote session for a specialist audience pays considerably more than a 15-minute unmoderated task.

terms.shortDef: Designing for the full range of human diversity.
terms.longDef: Where accessibility focuses on removing barriers for disabled people, inclusive design is the wider practice of building for varied abilities, contexts, languages and circumstances, and of involving those people in the work. Its central insight is that designing for a permanent constraint usually helps people with temporary and situational versions of it too. It is a method, not a compliance activity.
terms.example: One-handed operation designed for a person with limited mobility also serves someone holding a child or a coffee.
terms.misuse: Not a synonym for accessibility. Accessibility is a required outcome; inclusive design is one way of getting there.

terms.shortDef: New content loads automatically as the user reaches the bottom.
terms.longDef: It suits open-ended browsing where there is no destination, and it makes returning to a specific item hard, because position is lost. It also makes the page footer unreachable. A load-more button gives most of the benefit while keeping control and a stable end.
terms.example: A photo feed is a reasonable fit; a search results page where people compare options is not.
terms.misuse: Infinite scroll plus a footer containing important links is a well-known trap — the footer can never be reached.

terms.shortDef: How content is organised, labelled and connected.
terms.longDef: IA covers the structure beneath the interface: the groupings, the names, the hierarchy and the paths between things. It is mostly invisible when right and blamed for everything when wrong, because bad structure cannot be rescued by navigation design. It is also the most expensive thing to change after launch.
terms.example: Deciding whether billing lives under Account or under Settings, and what each of those words will mean to a customer.
terms.misuse: IA is not the navigation menu. The menu is one exposure of a structure that also drives search, URLs and permissions.

terms.shortDef: Participants agreeing to take part, knowing what will happen.
terms.longDef: Before a session begins, participants need to know what will be recorded, who will see it, how long it is kept and that they can stop at any time without losing their incentive. Consent has to be given in plain language, not buried in a legal wall. It is an ethical baseline and, for personal data, usually a legal one.
terms.example: "We'll record your screen and voice. Only the four people on this project will watch it, and we delete it after 90 days."

terms.shortDef: Formatting a field's value as the user types it.
terms.longDef: Masks add separators to card numbers, dates or phone numbers so the value stays readable and checkable. They must not reject characters the user reasonably types — a pasted number with spaces should be accepted and reformatted. Masks that move the cursor unpredictably are worse than no mask.
terms.example: Typing 4242424242424242 displays as 4242 4242 4242 4242, and pasting the spaced version works identically.
terms.misuse: Blocking input that does not match the mask is a common failure for international phone numbers and postcodes.

terms.shortDef: An observation that changes what the team will do.
terms.longDef: An insight explains a behaviour and implies an action; a finding that changes nothing is just a fact. Good ones name the tension — people want X but the design forces Y — and are traceable back to evidence. Teams that log insights without decisions accumulate a library nobody reads.
terms.example: "People treat the saved-card screen as a receipt, so they never notice the edit option" leads directly to a layout change.
terms.misuse: "Users want it to be simpler" is not an insight. It has no evidence, no mechanism and no action.

terms.shortDef: A designer specialising in behaviour: what happens when you act.
terms.longDef: Interaction design concerns states, transitions, feedback, timing and the logic of a control — the parts of a design that only exist in motion or in response. It is the discipline behind gestures, complex components and anything with more than two states. It sits closest to engineering of the design specialisms.
terms.example: Specifying what a card does on press, on long press, on drag, mid-flight, and when the network drops.

terms.shortDef: Building a product so it can be adapted to other languages and regions.
terms.longDef: It means no text baked into images, no assumptions about name or address shape, no concatenated sentences, and layouts that survive text expanding by a third or running right to left. It is preparation, done once; localisation is the per-locale work that follows. Retrofitting it is expensive and touches every screen.
terms.example: Leaving room for German labels roughly 35% longer than English, and mirroring the layout for Arabic.
terms.misuse: i18n is the preparation and l10n the adaptation. Teams that conflate them usually discover the difference during their first translation.

terms.shortDef: Repeated cycles of making, testing and revising.
terms.longDef: Each pass is deliberately small enough to be cheap to throw away, and each one is informed by evidence from the last. The value is compounding: three modest rounds beat one heroic attempt, because the second round knows something the first could not. It requires the organisation to accept that the first version is not the deliverable.
terms.example: A form is tested with five people, fixed, tested with five more, and fixed again inside two weeks.
terms.misuse: Shipping repeatedly is not iteration unless each release changes what you believe. Otherwise it is just a release cadence.

aliases: law of the internet user experience
terms.shortDef: People expect your product to work like the others they use.
terms.longDef: Users spend most of their time in other products, so their expectations are formed elsewhere. Matching established conventions means their existing knowledge transfers and they can start using yours immediately. Novelty is not free — every deviation from convention has to earn back the cost of relearning.
terms.example: A shopping cart icon in the top right, and a logo that returns to the homepage, work because a thousand other sites taught them.
terms.misuse: It is not an argument that you can never innovate. It says deviation must be worth its price, not that it is forbidden.

terms.shortDef: The progress someone is trying to make in their situation.
terms.longDef: The framing is that people hire a product to make progress, so the unit of analysis is the job rather than the person or the demographic. It surfaces unexpected competitors, because the alternatives are whatever else gets the job done — including a spreadsheet or doing nothing. Job stories are written as "when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]".
terms.example: "When I'm in a meeting and someone uses a term I don't know, I want to look it up without anyone noticing."
terms.misuse: A job is not a feature request or a task. "Filter by category" is a task; "decide quickly which option fits" is a job.

terms.shortDef: A timeline of a person's experience across touchpoints.
terms.longDef: A journey map lays out the stages someone passes through, what they do and feel at each, and where the pain concentrates. Its value is showing the gaps between channels that no single team owns. It must be grounded in research, or it is a diagram of the team's assumptions with an emotion line drawn on top.
terms.example: Mapping insurance claims end to end reveals the worst moment is the silence between submitting and hearing back.
terms.misuse: Not the same as a user flow. A journey spans channels and time; a flow is the steps inside one interface.

terms.shortDef: Sorting features into expected, desired and delighting.
terms.longDef: Basic expectations cause dissatisfaction when missing and no pleasure when present; performance features scale with how well they are done; delighters please when present and are not missed when absent. Categories migrate over time — today's delighter is next year's expectation. It is surveyed by asking how someone would feel both with and without a feature.
terms.example: Working offline is expected in a reference app; spaced-repetition revision is a delighter, for now.

terms.shortDef: Operating everything without a mouse or touch.
terms.longDef: Every interactive element must be reachable and usable by keyboard, in an order that matches the visual layout, with no trap that cannot be escaped. It is a requirement in itself and a proxy for switch access, voice control and screen readers, which all build on the same focus model. Unplugging the mouse for ten minutes is the cheapest audit available.
terms.example: Tabbing through a form, opening a dropdown with arrow keys, and closing a dialog with Escape back to the trigger.
terms.misuse: A custom control that is focusable but does nothing on Enter or Space is a keyboard failure, not a partial success.

terms.shortDef: A labelled region letting users jump straight to part of a page.
terms.longDef: Header, navigation, main, search and footer regions give screen-reader users a map and a way to skip whole sections in one gesture. They cost nothing when native elements are used. Multiple landmarks of the same type need distinct labels, or the map becomes ambiguous.
terms.example: Jumping directly to main content, bypassing a navigation region, using a single rotor gesture.

terms.shortDef: A model trained on text that predicts likely continuations.
terms.longDef: LLMs generate plausible text by predicting what follows, which makes them fluent, flexible and unreliable about facts in the same breath. They have a context limit, no inherent access to your data, and no way to know when they are wrong. Every design decision around them follows from those three properties.
terms.example: A feature that answers questions about your documents needs those documents supplied as context; the model does not know them.
terms.misuse: Fluency is not accuracy. Confident phrasing is a property of the model, not evidence that the answer is right.

terms.shortDef: People complete incomplete shapes into whole familiar forms.
terms.longDef: Given a partial outline, perception fills in the missing parts rather than seeing fragments. Logos and icons rely on it, and so does a carousel that shows a sliced card at the edge to imply more content. The implied whole must be obvious, or the result reads as broken rather than continuing.
terms.example: A horizontal list that cuts the fifth card in half tells you there is more to scroll without needing an arrow.

terms.shortDef: Elements inside a shared boundary are seen as one group.
terms.longDef: A border, a background panel or a card draws a region, and everything inside it is read as a unit — strongly enough to override proximity. That makes cards a blunt but reliable grouping device. Overused, the page becomes a set of boxes with no hierarchy between them.
terms.example: Two form fields inside a bordered panel read as one section even when a third field sits closer to them on the page.

terms.shortDef: People read complex images in the simplest form available.
terms.longDef: Perception resolves ambiguity toward the simplest, most stable interpretation, because that takes the least effort. Layouts built on regular shapes and consistent alignment are therefore processed faster and remembered better. Complex arrangements are not just harder to like — they are literally harder to see.
terms.example: A grid of aligned rectangles is understood at a glance; the same content in overlapping irregular shapes has to be studied.

terms.shortDef: Things placed close together are perceived as related.
terms.longDef: Spacing communicates grouping before any border or colour does, and it does so faster than reading. Getting proximity wrong is the single most common cause of confusing forms: a label sitting equidistant between two fields belongs to neither. Space is the cheapest grouping tool available.
terms.example: A label 4px above its input and 20px below the previous field reads unambiguously as belonging to the input below it.

terms.shortDef: Elements that look alike are perceived as belonging together.
terms.longDef: Shared shape, size, colour or typographic treatment implies a shared role. It is why every link in a page should look like every other link, and why making one button visually distinct is enough to mark it as different in kind. Inconsistent styling reads as meaningful difference even when none was intended.
terms.example: Underlined blue text is read as a link wherever it appears, so styling a heading that way makes people try to tap it.
terms.misuse: Similar-looking elements that behave differently are worse than inconsistent ones, because the visual promise is broken.

terms.shortDef: Content moving after it has already been rendered.
terms.longDef: Shifts happen when images, fonts, ads or late-loading data arrive without space reserved, and they cause mis-taps on exactly the wrong control. The fix is reserving dimensions in advance and matching placeholder sizes to real content. It is one of the most irritating defects to experience and one of the easiest to prevent.
terms.example: A banner loading above a list pushes the first row down just as the user taps it.

terms.shortDef: Loading content only when it is about to be needed.
terms.longDef: Deferring offscreen images, screens and code cuts the initial payload and gets people to the first useful moment sooner. It needs reserved space so nothing shifts, and a small lead time so content is ready just before it scrolls into view. Lazy-loading things that are immediately visible makes the experience worse, not better.
terms.example: Loading a list's images as they approach the viewport, with each slot already at its final height.
terms.misuse: Applying lazy loading to the first screen's hero image delays the very thing the metric measures.

terms.shortDef: The vertical space between lines of text.
terms.longDef: Body text usually wants around 1.4 to 1.6 times its size; large headings want proportionally less, because the gap looks bigger at scale. Too tight and lines interfere with each other, too loose and they stop reading as a paragraph. WCAG asks that users be able to increase it to 1.5 without breaking the layout.
terms.example: 17px body text set at 27px line height, with a 34px headword set at 40px.
terms.misuse: Applying one line-height multiplier across every size is the common shortcut, and it makes large text look gappy.

terms.shortDef: A question whose wording suggests the answer you want.
terms.longDef: Leading questions smuggle an assumption or a value judgement into the phrasing, and participants tend to cooperate with it. The damage is invisible: you get clean-looking data that only reflects your own hypothesis. The fix is neutral wording and open framing.
terms.example: "How easy was it to find the filter?" presumes it was easy. "Tell me about finding the filter" does not.

terms.shortDef: Designing through fast cycles of assumption, experiment and learning.
terms.longDef: Lean UX shifts the emphasis from deliverables to outcomes: state the assumption, build the smallest thing that tests it, measure, and decide. It suits environments with real access to users and frequent releases. It is often misapplied as a reason to skip research entirely rather than to make it smaller and faster.
terms.example: A one-week test of a pricing page assumption using a live variant, instead of a month producing a specification.
terms.misuse: Fewer deliverables is not less rigour. Lean UX replaces documentation with evidence, not with opinion.

terms.shortDef: How easily individual characters are told apart.
terms.longDef: Legibility is a property of the letterforms: whether capital I, lowercase l and the digit 1 are distinguishable, whether counters stay open at small sizes, whether the face survives low contrast. It is decided mostly at the point of choosing a typeface. It is the precondition for readability, not the same thing.
terms.example: A face where 0 and O differ clearly matters on a screen showing reference numbers.
terms.misuse: Legibility concerns characters; readability concerns whether a body of text is comfortable to read. Both are needed.

terms.shortDef: A symmetric agreement scale, usually five or seven points.
terms.longDef: Respondents rate agreement with a statement from strong disagreement to strong agreement, with a neutral midpoint. The scale must be balanced — equal positive and negative options — or the average is meaningless. Report the distribution alongside the mean, because a flat average can hide two opposed camps.
terms.example: "The pricing page told me what I would pay" — strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree.
terms.misuse: A single 1–5 star rating is not a Likert scale; a Likert item measures agreement with a statement, not overall preference.

terms.shortDef: An area whose updates are announced without moving focus.
terms.longDef: Live regions let a screen reader report changes the user did not navigate to — a result count updating, a toast appearing, an error arriving. Polite announcements wait for a pause; assertive ones interrupt and should be rare. Too many live regions make a product unusable through constant chatter.
terms.example: "12 results" announced politely as the user types, without pulling focus out of the search field.
terms.misuse: A visual toast with no live region is silent for screen-reader users, which is the most common version of this bug.

terms.shortDef: Adapting a product for a specific language and region.
terms.longDef: Beyond translation it covers date and number formats, currency, address forms, name order, units, imagery and legal requirements. Good localisation needs context for translators — a string with no note is guessed at. Machine translation without review reliably produces confident, wrong interface text.
terms.example: Switching to day-month-year, local currency, and a postcode field that matches the country's actual format.

terms.shortDef: Studying the same people repeatedly over an extended period.
terms.longDef: Measuring the same participants at intervals shows how behaviour changes as novelty wears off and habits form. It is the only reliable way to separate a real improvement from a temporary reaction to something new. The cost is time and participant drop-out.
terms.example: Tracking twelve new users weekly for two months shows the onboarding checklist is abandoned after day three.

terms.shortDef: How clearly controls correspond to the things they affect.
terms.longDef: Natural mapping arranges controls in the same spatial pattern as what they control, so the relationship needs no label or memory. The classic failure is a hob where four knobs sit in a row and four burners sit in a square. On screen it shows up whenever a control sits far from the thing it changes.
terms.example: Seat adjustment buttons shaped like a seat: push the top forward to tilt the backrest forward.

terms.shortDef: The width of a text column, counted in characters.
terms.longDef: Around 45 to 75 characters per line is comfortable for continuous reading; much longer and the eye loses its place returning to the left edge, much shorter and the rhythm breaks. On phones the constraint is the screen, so measure matters most on tablets and desktops where a column can otherwise run to 150 characters.
terms.example: Capping a definition column at roughly 560px keeps it near 65 characters at 17px.

terms.shortDef: What someone believes about how a system works.
terms.longDef: People build an internal story of what the system is doing and predict its behaviour from it, whether or not that story matches the implementation. Trouble appears at the gap between the two — the user's model says the file is saved, the system's model says it is not. Research exists largely to find those gaps.
terms.example: Many people believe deleting an email removes it permanently, which is why an unexpected "Trash" folder surprises them.
terms.misuse: Not the same as the conceptual model the designer intends. The mental model is whatever the user actually ended up with.

terms.shortDef: Structured data describing a piece of content.
terms.longDef: Categories, tags, dates, authorship and relationships are what make filtering, sorting, search and recommendation possible. Interfaces that promise powerful filtering on content with thin metadata cannot deliver it. Deciding the metadata is therefore a design decision, not a back-office one.
terms.example: Filtering terms by difficulty only works because every entry carries a difficulty value.

terms.shortDef: The small pieces of text that guide people through an interface.
terms.longDef: Button labels, hints, error text, empty states and confirmations do more usability work per word than anything else in a product. Buttons should name their outcome rather than say "submit", and hints should answer the question the field provokes. Small wording changes routinely move completion rates more than layout changes do.
terms.example: Changing a button from "Submit" to "Save term", with the confirmation reading "Saved."
terms.misuse: Microcopy is not decoration or personality. Jokes in an error message make a bad moment worse.

terms.shortDef: A small self-contained moment around a single action.
terms.longDef: A microinteraction has a trigger, rules, feedback and a result — a toggle flipping, a field validating, a like animating. They are where a product feels considered or careless, because they are the parts people touch most often. The feedback is the point; the animation is only one way to deliver it.
terms.example: Pulling to refresh: the trigger is the drag, the feedback is the tension and release, the result is fresh content.
terms.misuse: Not a synonym for animation. A microinteraction with no animation at all can still be well designed.

terms.shortDef: People hold about seven items in working memory at once.
terms.longDef: The original finding concerns immediate memory span, and later work puts the practical figure closer to four. The useful takeaway is not a magic number of menu items but that working memory is small, so interfaces should chunk information and avoid requiring people to carry values from screen to screen.
terms.example: Phone numbers are grouped in threes and fours because eleven separate digits exceed what most people can hold.
terms.misuse: Widely misquoted as "never show more than seven options". Miller was describing memory, not navigation.

terms.shortDef: The smallest release that tests a real assumption with real users.
terms.longDef: The point of an MVP is learning, not shipping less: it is the cheapest experiment that could change what you build next. The two failure modes are opposite — shipping something so thin it teaches nothing, and shipping a full product and calling it minimal. Viable means someone can genuinely get the value, not that it barely runs.
terms.example: A single flow released to one market to find out whether people will pay, before building the account system.
terms.misuse: Often used to mean version one with the quality removed. An MVP that damages trust has bought a lesson at full price.

terms.shortDef: A static, fully styled picture of what a screen will look like.
terms.longDef: A mockup applies real typography, colour, imagery and spacing to the structure a wireframe established. It is still static: nothing responds, and no flow is demonstrated. It is what stakeholders usually mean when they ask to "see the design", and what should be reviewed for visual craft and brand.
terms.example: The checkout screen with real product photography, final type sizes and the actual button colours, as a flat image.
terms.misuse: Showing a mockup is not testing a design. Without interaction, nobody can attempt the task it depicts.

terms.shortDef: A window that blocks the rest of the interface until dismissed.
terms.longDef: Modality forces a single decision by making everything else unavailable, which is why it suits confirmation of destructive actions and little else. It costs the user their context and, on small screens, most of the display. Focus must move into it and return to where it came from on close.
terms.example: "Delete this project and its 12 files? This cannot be undone", with Cancel and Delete, and nothing else reachable.
terms.misuse: Using a modal for content people need to refer back to forces them to memorise it. Use a page or a sheet instead.

terms.shortDef: A researcher is present, guiding tasks and asking follow-up questions.
terms.longDef: A facilitator runs the session live, in person or over a call, and can probe when something surprising happens. That flexibility is the whole value: you find out why someone hesitated, not just that they did. It costs more time per participant and introduces the risk that the facilitator nudges the outcome.
terms.example: A researcher shares a prototype over video, watches a participant hunt for the export button, then asks what they expected to find there.
terms.misuse: Being present is not the same as helping. A moderator who explains the interface has destroyed the finding they came for.

terms.shortDef: A collage that establishes visual direction before layout.
terms.longDef: Collecting type, colour, imagery and reference work in one place lets a team agree on a feeling before anyone commits to a screen. It is much cheaper to reject a direction here than after three mockups. Pairing each board with the adjectives it is meant to convey makes the conversation specific.
terms.example: Two boards labelled "authoritative and calm" and "friendly and quick", presented side by side to choose between.

terms.shortDef: Sorting work into must, should, could and won't have.
terms.longDef: The method's discipline is the last category: naming what will not be done in this release is what makes the first three meaningful. It suits scoping a fixed deadline better than ordering an ongoing backlog. It fails when everything is labelled must, which is the usual outcome without a facilitator.
terms.example: Agreeing that offline search is a must, flashcards a should, and cloud sync explicitly a won't for version one.

terms.shortDef: Designing how interfaces move between states.
terms.longDef: Motion in a product has jobs: showing where something came from, maintaining continuity, directing attention and confirming an action. Durations of roughly 150 to 350 milliseconds cover most interface transitions, with easing that starts fast and settles. Every motion decision needs a reduced-motion counterpart.
terms.example: A sheet rising from the control that opened it, so the origin of the new surface is never in doubt.
terms.misuse: Motion for delight alone becomes an obstacle by the hundredth time. Repeated interactions need the shortest motion that still reads.

terms.shortDef: Using more than one input or output channel together.
terms.longDef: Combining speech, touch, vision and haptics lets people use whichever channel suits the moment, which is both an accessibility gain and a practical one when hands or eyes are busy. Each mode needs to carry enough on its own, since any of them may be unavailable. Handing off mid-task between modes is the hard part.
terms.example: Asking a question aloud and receiving a spoken summary alongside a list on screen that can be scrolled.

terms.shortDef: Testing several elements at once to find the best combination.
terms.longDef: Rather than one change against a control, several variables are varied together and every combination gets traffic. It can reveal interactions an A/B test would miss — a headline that only works with a particular image. The cost is traffic: combinations multiply fast and each one needs its own sample.
terms.example: Three headlines crossed with two hero images gives six variants, each needing enough visitors to be judged.

terms.shortDef: The controls that let people move between parts of a product.
terms.longDef: Navigation has to answer three questions at once: where am I, where can I go, and how do I get back. Its labels are the most-read text in any product, which makes wording more important than styling. Structure comes first — no navigation design rescues a bad information architecture.
terms.example: A tab bar marking the current section, plus a back affordance on every pushed screen, answers all three questions.

terms.shortDef: Promoters minus detractors on a nought-to-ten recommendation question.
terms.longDef: Scores of nine and ten count as promoters, seven and eight are ignored, and nought to six are detractors; the score is the difference as a percentage. Its popularity comes from being comparable across companies rather than from being sensitive. The free-text follow-up is usually worth more than the number.
terms.example: An NPS of 22 is meaningless alone but informative against the same product's 8 last quarter, measured identically.
terms.misuse: NPS measures stated likelihood to recommend, not usability or satisfaction. It cannot tell you what to change.

terms.shortDef: Ten broad rules of thumb for judging interface usability.
terms.longDef: Ten principles — visibility of status, match with the real world, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimalist design, error recovery, and help — used as a checklist for expert review. They are deliberately general, which makes them a good lens and a poor specification. They identify candidate problems; testing confirms them.
terms.example: Reviewing a checkout against all ten produces a list like "no visible progress" and "error message does not say how to fix it".
terms.misuse: A heuristic evaluation is not a substitute for watching real users. Experts predict problems; they do not observe them.

terms.shortDef: A door whose design tells you to do the wrong thing.
terms.longDef: A handle that says pull on a door that opens outward is the canonical example of a signifier contradicting the mechanism. The name has become shorthand for any control whose appearance misleads about its behaviour. The failure is the design's, not the person's — which is the whole point of the term.
terms.example: A flat rectangle styled like a button that turns out to be a static label, next to a plain word that is the real action.

terms.shortDef: The single measure that best captures delivered value.
terms.longDef: A good North Star tracks the moment a user gets what they came for, not the money that follows. It aligns teams by giving them one number they all influence, supported by a small set of contributing measures. A badly chosen one is worse than none, because a whole organisation optimises it.
terms.example: "Terms looked up and understood per weekly active user" beats "app opens", which rewards confusion.
terms.misuse: Revenue is a lagging outcome, not a North Star. It moves for reasons the product team cannot see or influence.

terms.shortDef: A temporary lift in engagement caused purely by something being new.
terms.longDef: When an interface changes, people click around to see what happened, which inflates early metrics. The mirror image is the change-aversion dip, where familiar users perform worse for a while. Both fade, so experiments on visible changes need to run long enough for behaviour to settle.
terms.example: A redesigned tab bar shows a 20% jump in taps in week one and returns to baseline by week three.
terms.misuse: Reading week-one numbers as proof a redesign worked is one of the most common ways teams fool themselves.

terms.shortDef: People behave differently because they know they are watched.
terms.longDef: Participants try harder, read more carefully and complain less when a researcher is present. It cannot be eliminated, only reduced: emphasise that the design is being tested rather than the person, stay quiet, and treat effortful behaviour in a session as a floor on the difficulty, not a ceiling.
terms.example: A participant reads every word of an error message in a lab and admits they would normally close the tab.

terms.shortDef: Prefer the simplest option that still does the job.
terms.longDef: Among designs that meet the requirement, the one with the fewest parts is usually the best bet: fewer states to build, fewer things to explain, fewer ways to break. It is a tie-breaker rather than a design method — it applies once the options all work. The trap is treating "fewest elements on screen" as the goal instead of "fewest necessary".
terms.example: Choosing a single text field with inline validation over a wizard, when both collect the same three values.
terms.misuse: Simplicity for its own sake produces hidden functionality and mystery-meat icons. Removing labels is not simplification.

terms.shortDef: Treating the network as an enhancement, not a requirement.
terms.longDef: Data lives locally and syncs when a connection exists, so the interface never waits on a request it does not need. It removes whole categories of loading and error state, and it makes the product usable on a train or a plane. The cost is handling sync conflicts and deciding what a stale local copy is allowed to do.
terms.example: A dictionary that ships its content in the bundle, reads from a local database, and checks for updates in the background.
terms.misuse: Caching responses is not offline-first. The test is whether the product works from a cold start with no network at all.

terms.shortDef: A qualitative objective paired with measurable results.
terms.longDef: The objective states what you are trying to achieve and the key results define how you will know, in numbers. Well-written key results describe outcomes rather than deliverables — shipping a feature is not a result. They work as an alignment tool and fail when tied directly to individual performance reviews.
terms.example: Objective: people trust our search. Key result: no-result searches fall from 14% to under 5%.
terms.misuse: "Launch the new search" is a task masquerading as a key result. It can be completed without anything improving.

terms.shortDef: One continuous experience across every channel a customer uses.
terms.longDef: The test is whether a task started in one place can be finished in another without repeating yourself. That requires shared state and shared language, which is usually an organisational problem rather than a design one. Multichannel means being present in several places; omnichannel means those places are joined.
terms.example: Starting an application on a phone and finishing it in a branch, where the assistant sees exactly what was entered.
terms.misuse: Having an app, a website and a call centre is multichannel. Without shared state it is not omnichannel.

terms.shortDef: Getting a new user to their first useful outcome.
terms.longDef: The goal is not to explain the product but to get someone to value quickly, ideally by doing something real rather than watching a tour. Explanations work best delivered in context, at the moment they are needed. Onboarding that must be completed before anything can be tried fights the way people actually learn software.
terms.example: A notes app that opens with a new note ready to type, and explains sync the first time a second device appears.
terms.misuse: A carousel of feature screenshots before signup is skipped by most people and remembered by almost none.

terms.shortDef: Showing the result immediately, before the server confirms it.
terms.longDef: The interface assumes success and updates at once, reconciling later if the request fails. It removes waiting from actions that almost always succeed, such as liking or reordering. It requires a genuine plan for failure — a silent revert leaves the user believing something happened that did not.
terms.example: A bookmark fills in the moment it is tapped; if the write fails, it un-fills with a message explaining why.
terms.misuse: Optimistic updates for actions that often fail, or that involve money, trade trust for a small gain in speed.

terms.shortDef: Splitting a long list into numbered pages.
terms.longDef: Pagination gives a sense of how much there is, makes positions stable enough to return to, and keeps each request small. It costs an interaction per page and interrupts browsing. It suits result sets people work through deliberately rather than feeds they graze.
terms.example: Search results showing "page 2 of 14" so the user can judge whether to refine the query instead of scrolling.

terms.shortDef: People start using software immediately rather than reading instructions.
terms.longDef: Users skip the manual and the tour because they want to get something done now, even though reading would be faster overall. Designing around it means putting help where the difficulty happens rather than up front, and making the first attempt recoverable. Onboarding that must be read to be survived will not be read.
terms.example: A tooltip that appears the first time someone opens the filter panel beats a five-screen tour shown at signup.
terms.misuse: The answer is not more forced tutorials. It is an interface that can be learned by trying.

terms.shortDef: Work expands to fill the time available for it.
terms.longDef: Given a generous deadline, a task consumes the whole of it. In interface terms, if a process is allowed to feel long, users will settle into that pace and expect it. Constraining the time — through defaults, autofill and shorter forms — often improves both speed and satisfaction.
terms.example: A tax form that pre-fills known data is finished faster, and users report it as less onerous, than the same form left blank.

terms.shortDef: Designing with the people affected, not just for them.
terms.longDef: Users join the design work itself — sketching, arranging, deciding priorities — rather than only reacting to finished proposals. It surfaces constraints outsiders cannot see and builds ownership among the people who will live with the result. The designer's job shifts to facilitating and then editing.
terms.example: Nurses rearrange printed cards of a handover screen until the order matches how they actually give a report.
terms.misuse: Participants are experts on their own work, not on interface design. Their layout is input, not a specification.

terms.shortDef: People judge an experience by its peak and its ending.
terms.longDef: Memory of an experience is dominated by its most intense moment and by how it finished, not by the average or the duration. That makes the last screen of a flow disproportionately important, and it makes one bad moment expensive even in an otherwise smooth journey. Design the ending deliberately rather than letting it be whatever is left.
terms.example: A ride-hailing app ending on a clean receipt and a driver thank-you leaves a better memory than the same trip ending on a survey.
terms.misuse: It does not license a painful middle. A high peak of frustration is exactly what gets remembered.

terms.shortDef: How fast something feels, regardless of measured time.
terms.longDef: Feedback within a hundred milliseconds, skeletons that show shape, optimistic updates and prefetching all make identical elapsed time feel shorter. Occupied waits feel shorter than idle ones, and known waits shorter than unknown. It is not a substitute for being fast, but it is often the cheaper half of the improvement.
terms.example: Rendering cached results instantly while fresher ones load makes a 600ms request feel immediate.
terms.misuse: Perceived performance work that hides a genuine failure — a spinner over a request that never returns — spends trust.

terms.shortDef: How quickly a product responds and completes work.
terms.longDef: Performance is a usability property, not a technical afterthought: it changes task success, bounce and satisfaction more reliably than most visual decisions. It should be measured on the devices and networks the audience actually has, not on a developer's machine. Design choices — image weight, font loading, animation — are among its main drivers.
terms.example: Cutting a bundle from ten megabytes to four by importing only the font weights the product uses.

terms.shortDef: A research-based character standing for a group of users.
terms.longDef: A persona compresses patterns found in research into one memorable figure with goals, context and constraints, so a team can ask what that person needs rather than what "the user" needs. It is only as good as the research beneath it. Demographic detail is usually decoration; the goals and behaviours are the substance.
terms.example: "Priya, ward pharmacist, checks stock between rounds on a shared tablet and cannot log in twice in one shift."
terms.misuse: A persona invented in a workshop is a proto-persona, and should be labelled as such so nobody cites it as evidence.

terms.shortDef: Changing what someone sees based on what is known about them.
terms.longDef: Personalisation can be explicit, from stated preferences, or implicit, inferred from behaviour. Implicit adaptation risks making the interface unpredictable and unlearnable, and it can feel intrusive when the inference is visibly accurate. Explaining why something is shown, and allowing it to be corrected, is what keeps it acceptable.
terms.example: Surfacing recently viewed terms is welcome; silently reordering the main navigation per user is not.
terms.misuse: Personalisation is not customisation. One is the system deciding; the other is the user deciding.

terms.shortDef: Writing so people understand it the first time they read it.
terms.longDef: Plain language means short sentences, common words, active voice and the important thing first. It is not dumbing down: experts read plain writing faster too, and under stress everyone's reading ability drops. Legal and technical accuracy can almost always survive the rewrite.
terms.example: "We will refund you within five working days" instead of "reimbursement shall be effected within the stated period".

terms.shortDef: How things are normally done on a specific operating system.
terms.longDef: iOS and Android differ in navigation, back behaviour, typography, sheet behaviour and system gestures, and users of each have expectations built by every other app they own. Cross-platform products decide how much to unify and how much to respect each platform. Back behaviour and system gestures are the ones you break at your peril.
terms.example: Android's system back gesture must dismiss a sheet; ignoring it makes the app feel broken rather than distinctive.

terms.shortDef: A curated set of work showing how you think, not just what you made.
terms.longDef: Reviewers look for the problem, the constraints, what you decided and why, what you would do differently, and what actually happened. Three deep case studies beat twelve screenshots. Being explicit about your own contribution on team projects matters more than the polish of the final image.
terms.example: A case study that opens with the business problem and the constraint, and closes with the measured result and a regret.
terms.misuse: A gallery of finished screens with no reasoning is a gallery, not a portfolio.

terms.shortDef: The place a product occupies relative to its alternatives.
terms.longDef: Positioning decides which comparison a customer makes, which sets their expectations about price, depth and audience. It is chosen by naming the market you are in and the alternative you are better than for a specific job. Design carries it: what a product looks like and how much it explains signal who it is for.
terms.example: A reference tool positioned against a PDF glossary competes on speed; positioned against a course, it competes on depth.

terms.shortDef: Accept input liberally, produce output conservatively.
terms.longDef: Borrowed from network protocol design, it argues that a system should tolerate whatever form the input arrives in and be strict about what it emits. For interfaces this means accepting a phone number with or without spaces, and a date in whatever order the person typed it, rather than rejecting it. The strictness belongs in your own output, not in the demands you make of people.
terms.example: A card field that silently strips spaces and dashes instead of showing "invalid card number".
terms.misuse: Being liberal is not the same as being silent. Show what you understood the input to mean.

terms.shortDef: WCAG's four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust.
terms.longDef: Content must be perceivable through more than one sense, operable by more than one input, understandable in language and behaviour, and robust enough to work with assistive technology now and later. Every WCAG criterion sits under one of the four. It is a useful diagnostic: when something fails, naming which principle broke usually points at the fix.
terms.example: A video with no captions fails perceivable; a menu that only opens on hover fails operable.

terms.shortDef: Deciding what to do next, and what not to do at all.
terms.longDef: Frameworks such as RICE, MoSCoW and the Kano model exist to make the reasoning visible and the trade-offs arguable, not to produce an answer mechanically. Whatever the method, the useful output is an explicit ranking with the assumptions written down. The hardest and most valuable part is deciding what is dropped.
terms.example: Scoring twelve candidate features on reach, impact, confidence and effort, then discussing the three where the scores surprised everyone.
terms.misuse: A framework's number is an argument, not a verdict. Teams that stop debating after scoring have outsourced judgement to arithmetic.

terms.shortDef: Treating privacy as a default, built in from the start.
terms.longDef: The principles are collecting only what is needed, keeping it only as long as it is useful, defaulting to the most protective setting, and being clear about what happens. Designers control much of this through what a form asks for and how a permission is requested. Data you never collected cannot leak.
terms.example: Logging searches that found nothing on the device only, so the content backlog exists without any data leaving the phone.

terms.shortDef: Deciding which problem you are actually solving.
terms.longDef: The frame determines the range of solutions anyone will consider, which makes it the highest-leverage decision in a project. Reframing — moving from "make the form shorter" to "reduce the reasons people abandon it" — often unlocks better answers than any amount of ideation inside the original frame. Write the frame down, because unwritten frames go unchallenged.
terms.example: "People cannot find the export button" reframed as "people need this data in a spreadsheet" leads to scheduled email exports instead.
terms.misuse: A problem statement containing a solution is not a frame. "Users need a dashboard" has already decided the answer.

terms.shortDef: A designer accountable for outcomes, not just screens.
terms.longDef: The title usually signals involvement from problem definition through to measurement: research, interaction, interface and the business case around them. It became common as companies wanted designers who could argue about what to build, not only how it should look. In practice it often means a UX designer expected to also engage with metrics and strategy.
terms.example: Deciding with a PM that a feature should not be built, based on research, and proposing a smaller change instead.

terms.shortDef: Product, design and engineering leading a team together.
terms.longDef: The three roles share responsibility for what gets built: desirability, viability and feasibility argued in the same room rather than passed between functions. It works when all three are involved from problem definition. It degrades into a relay when design joins after the decision has been made.
terms.example: A PM, designer and tech lead jointly deciding to cut scope after a prototype test rather than escalating.

terms.shortDef: Evidence that a market genuinely wants what you built.
terms.longDef: It shows up as retention that flattens rather than decays, organic growth, and users who would be upset if the product vanished. Before it, adding features rarely helps; after it, the constraint becomes scale. It is a state you can lose as a market shifts, not a milestone you pass once.
terms.example: Week-eight retention settling at a stable plateau instead of continuing to fall is the usual first signal.
terms.misuse: Growth from paid acquisition is not fit. It measures how much you spent, not how much people wanted it.

terms.shortDef: A signal that the system is working, and how far along it is.
terms.longDef: Determinate indicators show proportion completed and suit anything over a few seconds; indeterminate spinners only say that something is happening. Below about a second, showing nothing is better than a flash of loading. Over about ten, say what is happening and roughly how long it will take.
terms.example: "Uploading 3 of 12 files" tells the user more than a spinning circle, and lets them decide whether to wait.
terms.misuse: A spinner with no timeout is the most common way an interface silently fails. Every wait needs an end state.

terms.shortDef: Showing what most people need, with the rest one step away.
terms.longDef: Common options stay visible while advanced ones move behind a clearly labelled control. Done well it reduces load without reducing capability, and the label has to promise what is behind it. Done badly it becomes hidden functionality that only the people who wrote it can find.
terms.example: A share sheet showing three destinations and "More options", rather than twenty at once.
terms.misuse: Hiding something everyone needs is not progressive disclosure, it is an extra tap for the whole audience.

terms.shortDef: Build a working baseline first, then layer improvements on top.
terms.longDef: The core content and function work with the simplest capabilities, and richer behaviour is added where supported. It produces resilient products: a failed script degrades a feature rather than emptying the page. It also tends to produce better accessibility, because the baseline is usually semantic and keyboard-operable.
terms.example: A form that submits and works without JavaScript, then gains inline validation when the script loads.
terms.misuse: Not the same as graceful degradation, which starts from the full experience and removes parts for weaker clients.

terms.shortDef: A website that can be installed and work offline.
terms.longDef: A PWA adds an installable icon, offline capability and background updates to a normal web app, without an app store. It suits products where discovery through a link matters more than deep device integration. Capabilities still lag native on iOS, particularly around notifications and background work.
terms.example: A reference site that installs to the home screen and keeps working on the underground.

terms.shortDef: The instruction and context given to a model to produce an output.
terms.longDef: A prompt combines the user's request with instructions, examples and context the product supplies behind the scenes. Much of the design work is deciding what the product adds silently — tone, constraints, format — so the user does not have to. Exposing a blank prompt box puts the burden on the user and produces wildly variable results.
terms.example: A rewrite feature offering "shorter", "plainer" and "more formal" rather than an empty instruction field.
terms.misuse: Prompt engineering is not a substitute for interface design. If the user has to phrase it well, the product has not done its job.

terms.shortDef: A persona built from team assumptions, pending research.
terms.longDef: Proto-personas capture what the team currently believes about its users, explicitly as hypotheses to be checked. They are useful for surfacing disagreement early and for prioritising which research to run first. The danger is that they harden into fact once they are printed on the wall.
terms.example: A kickoff workshop produces three proto-personas; two survive the first round of interviews and one turns out not to exist.

terms.shortDef: Something interactive enough for a person to attempt a task.
terms.longDef: A prototype simulates behaviour — taps lead somewhere, states change — which is what makes it testable. Fidelity is a choice per question: paper is enough to test a flow, a coded prototype may be needed to test a gesture or a transition. It exists to answer a question and then be thrown away.
terms.example: A linked set of screens where tapping "Pay" shows a processing state and then a receipt, used in a usability test.
terms.misuse: The wireframe / mockup / prototype distinction is about what each demonstrates: structure, appearance, and behaviour. A prototype can be at any visual fidelity.

terms.shortDef: Dragging a list downward to reload its contents.
terms.longDef: The gesture became a convention because it maps neatly onto the idea of pulling new content into view, and because it needs no permanent control. It is undiscoverable on its own and unavailable to keyboard and switch users. Products that rely on it should also refresh automatically and offer a visible control.
terms.example: A feed that refreshes on pull, refreshes on returning to the screen, and has a refresh item in its menu.

terms.shortDef: Research that explains why, through observation and conversation.
terms.longDef: Qualitative work produces descriptions, quotes and observed behaviour rather than numbers. It is how you discover problems, understand motivation and learn the words people use. It cannot tell you how common something is, so it pairs naturally with a measurement afterwards.
terms.example: Six interviews reveal that people abandon signup because they cannot tell whether the trial charges them; analytics then shows how many.
terms.misuse: Counting qualitative findings — "four out of six said" — implies a precision the sample cannot support.

terms.shortDef: Research that measures how much or how many.
terms.longDef: Quantitative work counts behaviour or responses across a sample big enough to generalise. It answers scale questions — how many people hit this, how much did it move — and supports comparison over time. It rarely explains a result, which is why a surprising number is a prompt for qualitative follow-up.
terms.example: A benchmark study measures task success across 120 participants before and after a navigation change.

terms.shortDef: How comfortably a body of text can be read at length.
terms.longDef: Readability comes from measure, leading, size, contrast, alignment and the language itself. A perfectly legible typeface set in a 140-character line at tight leading is still unreadable. It is also affected by writing: shorter sentences and common words genuinely reduce effort.
terms.example: The same paragraph becomes markedly easier at 65 characters per line with 1.55 leading than at 140 characters with 1.2.

terms.shortDef: Showing options beats making people remember them.
terms.longDef: Recognising something on screen is far easier than retrieving it from memory unprompted. Interfaces should keep needed information visible or one glance away, rather than requiring users to carry it between steps. It is the argument for visible menus over memorised commands, and for showing what was entered before asking to confirm it.
terms.example: A search field that shows recent searches beneath it, rather than an empty box you must remember what to type into.
terms.misuse: It does not mean showing everything at once. Showing options on demand still counts as recognition.

terms.shortDef: A system that suggests items it predicts you will want.
terms.longDef: Recommendations are generated from similarity between items, between users, or both, and they shape what most people ever see in a large catalogue. Design decisions include how much diversity to keep, how to handle a brand-new user, and whether to explain each suggestion. Optimising purely for immediate clicks tends to narrow what anyone is shown over time.
terms.example: "Related terms" derived from cross-links rather than popularity, so rarely visited entries remain reachable.

terms.shortDef: Finding, screening and scheduling the right research participants.
terms.longDef: Recruitment decides whose reality your findings describe, which makes it the highest-leverage and most commonly rushed part of a study. Sources include panels, customer lists, intercepts on your own site and community groups, each with its own bias. Budget incentives and no-shows into the plan.
terms.example: Recruiting only from the in-app support queue produces a study about people who already had a problem.

terms.shortDef: Honouring the system setting that suppresses animation.
terms.longDef: Large parallax, zooming transitions and looping movement can trigger nausea, dizziness and migraine for people with vestibular disorders. When the setting is on, replace motion with an instant change or a simple fade rather than removing the feedback entirely. The setting exists on every major platform and is trivial to read.
terms.example: A card flip becomes an immediate swap, and staggered list entrances render instantly, when reduced motion is on.
terms.misuse: Reduced motion does not mean no feedback. Silently dropping the transition and its result leaves the user unsure what happened.

terms.shortDef: A searchable store of past studies, clips and findings.
terms.longDef: A repository keeps evidence findable after the project ends, so the next team does not re-run the same study. It works when entries are tagged consistently and each finding links to its source clip. It fails when it becomes a dumping ground for raw recordings nobody has time to watch.
terms.example: Searching "delivery estimate" returns four findings across three years, each with a 40-second clip and the study it came from.

terms.shortDef: The systems that make research repeatable: recruiting, tools, consent, storage.
terms.longDef: ResearchOps handles the logistics so researchers spend their time on questions rather than scheduling. Typical scope covers participant panels, incentives, consent and retention policy, tooling, templates and the repository. It becomes necessary at the point where more than a couple of people are running studies.
terms.example: A standing panel of 400 opted-in customers with tracked incentive budgets cuts study lead time from three weeks to four days.

terms.shortDef: One layout that reflows to fit any screen size.
terms.longDef: Content and layout adapt fluidly to the space available, rather than being switched between fixed designs. Doing it well means deciding what reorders, what collapses and what is dropped, at each size. Orientation, window resizing on desktop, and text scaling all count as size changes too.
terms.example: A two-column term page that stacks on a phone and caps its reading column on a tablet.
terms.misuse: Responsive is not the same as mobile-friendly. A layout can resize perfectly and still have unreachable touch targets.

terms.shortDef: The share of users who come back after a given period.
terms.longDef: Retention is the closest single measure to whether a product delivers value, because people return to things that work. It should be read as a curve by cohort: a curve that flattens indicates a group who genuinely need the product, while one that decays to zero indicates none. The natural frequency matters — a tax tool that is used yearly should not be judged weekly.
terms.example: Week-one retention of 40% falling to a flat 22% by week six is a healthier signal than 60% still falling.

terms.shortDef: Supplying a model with retrieved documents to answer from.
terms.longDef: Relevant material is looked up first and passed to the model as context, so answers are grounded in specific sources rather than in training data. It reduces invention and, importantly for design, makes citation possible — you can show which passage an answer came from. Retrieval quality then becomes the limiting factor, and a failed retrieval is invisible to the user unless the interface says so.
terms.example: A help assistant that answers from your own documentation and links the paragraph it used.

terms.shortDef: A score from reach, impact, confidence and effort.
terms.longDef: Reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort, produces a comparable number per item. Its value is forcing the confidence term into the open, which is usually where teams are fooling themselves. Its weakness is false precision — the inputs are estimates and the output looks like a measurement.
terms.example: A feature reaching 8,000 users a quarter with modest impact can outrank a beloved idea reaching 200.
terms.misuse: Comparing RICE scores calculated by different people with different scales compares nothing at all.

terms.shortDef: A communicated plan of what a team intends to work on.
terms.longDef: A roadmap's job is alignment: what we are betting on, roughly when, and why. Outcome-based roadmaps that name problems age better than feature lists with dates, which become promises the moment they are shared. Confidence should decrease visibly the further out it goes.
terms.example: Three horizons: committed this quarter, likely next, and problems being explored with no dates attached.
terms.misuse: A roadmap of dated features is a delivery schedule. Presenting it as a plan turns every learning into a broken promise.

terms.shortDef: The screen region not covered by system UI or hardware cutouts.
terms.longDef: Notches, rounded corners, status bars and home indicators all take space that content must avoid, and the amounts differ per device and orientation. Backgrounds should extend beneath them while interactive content stays inside. Ignoring insets is what puts a button under the home indicator, where it cannot be tapped.
terms.example: A tab bar padded by the bottom inset so its labels sit above the home indicator on every phone.

terms.shortDef: How many participants a study needs to answer its question.
terms.longDef: Qualitative and quantitative studies need very different numbers. Five participants per audience will expose most severe usability problems because problems repeat; measuring a conversion difference of one percentage point may need tens of thousands of sessions. Decide the number from the question, not from the budget.
terms.example: Five participants for a formative usability test; 20 or more per group for a benchmark you intend to report as a number.
terms.misuse: "Five users is enough" is advice about finding problems, not about measuring anything.

terms.shortDef: When the people studied do not represent the people affected.
terms.longDef: Every recruiting channel skews: in-app surveys reach only active users, panels reach frequent participants, and support queues reach people already in trouble. The bias is invisible in the data itself, which is why the recruiting method belongs in every report. It matters most when you generalise a percentage.
terms.example: A satisfaction survey shown only inside the app misses everyone who gave up before installing it.

terms.shortDef: The point where new participants stop revealing anything new.
terms.longDef: In qualitative work you keep recruiting until the last few sessions produce only repetition. That is the signal you have covered the range within this audience. Saturation is per audience: reaching it with existing customers says nothing about people who have never signed up.
terms.example: By the seventh interview every pain point mentioned has already appeared twice, so the eighth is scheduled as a check rather than a discovery.

terms.shortDef: A short narrative of someone using the product to reach a goal.
terms.longDef: A scenario names the person, their situation, their goal and the constraints acting on them, then describes what happens. It keeps design conversations concrete and doubles as the script for usability test tasks. The constraints are the useful part — a scenario with no pressure in it describes nobody.
terms.example: "Priya has four minutes between rounds, one hand free, and needs to confirm a dose she half-remembers."

terms.shortDef: Software that speaks interface content aloud.
terms.longDef: A screen reader builds a linear model of the interface from its structure — roles, names, states — and lets the user move through it by element, heading or landmark. What it announces comes from code, not appearance, so a visually obvious button with no accessible name is announced as "button". Testing with the real thing takes minutes and finds problems no checklist does.
terms.example: Turning on VoiceOver and completing a search, reading a definition and saving it without looking at the screen.
terms.misuse: Screen reader users do not read pages top to bottom. Most navigate by headings and landmarks, which is why structure matters.

terms.shortDef: A short questionnaire that decides who qualifies for a study.
terms.longDef: The screener filters applicants down to the people whose experience matters for this question, and filters out professional participants who answer whatever gets them in. Good screeners ask about recent behaviour rather than identity, and hide which answer qualifies. A study is only as good as who is in the room.
terms.example: "Which of these have you done in the last 30 days?" with the qualifying behaviour buried among plausible distractors.
terms.misuse: Asking "do you shop online often?" invites people to say yes. Ask how many times they did it last month.

terms.shortDef: A visual hint that there is more content below or beside.
terms.longDef: People scroll readily, but only when something tells them there is more. Content cut off at the fold, a partially visible next card, or a fading edge all signal continuation. A section that ends exactly at the viewport edge reads as the end of the page.
terms.example: A horizontal row that shows half of the next item, so the row obviously continues past the screen edge.

terms.shortDef: Letting people find content by typing what they want.
terms.longDef: Search is how people who know what they want bypass your structure, and how people whose vocabulary differs from yours get anywhere at all. It needs synonym handling, tolerance for typos and a useful no-results state. Logging queries that return nothing is the cheapest content research available.
terms.example: A dictionary that matches aliases as well as headwords finds "split test" when the entry is filed under "A/B test".
terms.misuse: Zero-result pages that only say "no results" waste the most informative moment in the whole product.

terms.shortDef: Splitting users into groups that behave differently.
terms.longDef: Averages hide the thing you need: a flat overall number often contains one group improving and another collapsing. Behavioural segments — new versus returning, mobile versus desktop, power versus occasional — usually explain more than demographic ones. Every headline metric deserves at least one split before anyone acts on it.
terms.example: A neutral overall result splits into a 9% gain for new users and a 6% loss for returning ones.

terms.shortDef: Radio buttons, checkboxes and switches, each with a distinct meaning.
terms.longDef: Radio buttons choose one from several and cannot be unset once chosen; checkboxes allow any number including none; switches turn one setting on or off and take effect immediately. Using the wrong one misleads people about what will happen. A switch implies instant effect, so a switch inside a form with a Save button is a contradiction.
terms.example: Delivery speed is radio buttons, marketing preferences are checkboxes, and dark mode is a switch.
terms.misuse: Checkboxes used for a single either-or choice hide the alternative, since an unticked box does not state what happens instead.

terms.shortDef: Using elements for their meaning, not just their appearance.
terms.longDef: A real button, heading or list carries role, state and keyboard behaviour for free, across every assistive technology and platform. Recreating them from generic containers means reimplementing all of that, usually incompletely. The first rule of ARIA is that not using ARIA is better — use the native element.
terms.example: A button element responds to Enter and Space, is focusable, and is announced as a button, with no extra code.
terms.misuse: A styled div with a click handler looks identical and is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users.

terms.shortDef: Version numbers that communicate the size of a change.
terms.longDef: Major.minor.patch, where a major bump signals a breaking change, a minor adds capability compatibly, and a patch fixes something.
