Design systems use it to tell consuming teams whether an upgrade is safe. Renaming a token or changing a component's default is a breaking change even though nothing crashed.
terms.example: Removing a Button variant means 3.0.0, while adding a new size is 2.4.0.

terms.shortDef: People remember the first and last items in a list best.
terms.longDef: Items at the start benefit from primacy and items at the end from recency, while the middle is where things go to be forgotten. It argues for placing the most important actions at the two ends of a navigation set. It also explains why a critical option buried mid-menu goes unused.
terms.example: Mobile tab bars put the primary destination first and the account last, leaving lower-traffic sections in the middle.

terms.shortDef: Building the page on the server rather than in the browser.
terms.longDef: Server rendering sends usable HTML immediately, which helps first paint, weak devices and search indexing; client rendering builds the page in the browser, which suits highly interactive apps after load. Most products now mix them. For designers it decides how much appears before scripts run, and therefore what the first frame looks like.
terms.example: An article rendered on the server is readable before any script executes; a dashboard is not.

terms.shortDef: A journey map extended to show the backstage work behind it.
terms.longDef: Above the line of visibility sits what the customer experiences; below it sit staff actions, systems and policies that produce it. It is the tool for diagnosing why a customer-facing problem exists, because the cause is usually backstage. It requires operations people in the room, not just design.
terms.example: A blueprint of a refund shows the four-day wait is caused by a manual approval queue nobody in design knew about.

terms.shortDef: Designing the whole service, including the parts users never see.
terms.longDef: Service design covers the people, processes and systems that produce an experience across every channel — app, phone, letter, counter. It treats staff-facing tools and policies as design material, because a customer-facing problem is usually caused backstage. Its characteristic artefact is the service blueprint.
terms.example: Redesigning a returns service means changing the warehouse process and the refund policy, not only the returns screen.

terms.shortDef: A replay of a real user's interactions with the product.
terms.longDef: Replays show hesitation, rage clicks and repeated attempts that no funnel captures, which makes them the fastest way to understand a drop-off you have already located. They carry real privacy weight: inputs must be masked and consent handled properly. Watching them at random is a poor use of time — sample from a known problem.
terms.example: Watching ten sessions that abandoned at payment reveals people tapping a non-interactive total, expecting a breakdown.
terms.misuse: Replays show what happened, not why. They generate hypotheses to test, not conclusions.

terms.shortDef: The cue that advertises an available action.
terms.longDef: Signifiers are the marks that tell someone what to do: an underline, a chevron, a shadow, the word "Menu". They exist for communication, and they are what design mostly manipulates, since the underlying affordance is often already there. Flat interfaces went wrong by removing signifiers while keeping the affordances.
terms.example: The chevron on a list row signifies that tapping it opens something, even though the whole row was always tappable.
terms.misuse: Not interchangeable with affordance. A door still affords pushing when the "PUSH" sticker falls off — you just cannot tell.

terms.shortDef: A tree diagram of every page and how they nest.
terms.longDef: The sitemap makes the hierarchy visible: what sits at the top level, what is buried three clicks down, and where duplication has crept in. It is the artefact most often tested with tree testing before any interface exists. On large products it is generated from the taxonomy rather than drawn by hand.
terms.example: A sitemap showing that help content exists in three places under different names, none of them linked to each other.

terms.shortDef: Grey placeholders in the shape of content that is loading.
terms.longDef: Showing the layout before the data arrives makes a wait feel shorter than a spinner does, because progress appears to be happening and the page does not jump when content lands. It only helps for short waits; beyond a few seconds people need a real progress signal. The skeleton must match the real layout or the shift is worse.
terms.example: Three grey bars where the article title and two lines of summary will appear, replaced in place when loaded.
terms.misuse: A skeleton that never resolves is worse than a spinner, because it looks like content that failed to render.

terms.shortDef: A fast, rough drawing used to think and to share options.
terms.longDef: Sketching is the cheapest way to externalise an idea, which is why it belongs early and in volume. Its roughness is protective: nobody argues about the corner radius of a pencil line. The skill being practised is generating variety, not drawing well.
terms.example: Twelve pencil thumbnails of a dashboard on one page, three of which are worth turning into wireframes.

terms.shortDef: A link that jumps past repeated navigation to the main content.
terms.longDef: Usually the first focusable element and visually hidden until focused, it saves keyboard users from tabbing through the same navigation on every page. It must actually move focus, not just scroll. On apps with landmark regions it matters less, but it remains the cheapest fix for repetitive navigation.
terms.example: Pressing Tab on load reveals "Skip to main content", which moves focus straight into the page body.

terms.shortDef: Pre-selecting the option most people will want.
terms.longDef: Defaults are the most powerful control in an interface, because most people accept them. Setting them from context — country from locale, today's date, the last-used option — removes work without removing choice. The ethical line is that a default must serve the user, not just the business.
terms.example: A delivery form pre-filling the saved address, with a visible option to send it somewhere else.
terms.misuse: A pre-ticked marketing box is a default working against the user, and is unlawful in several jurisdictions.

terms.shortDef: A fixed set of spacing values used everywhere in a design.
terms.longDef: Building every gap from multiples of a base unit — usually four or eight — makes rhythm consistent and removes an arbitrary decision from every component. It also makes design and code agree, since both reference the same steps. The scale needs enough small steps to handle text spacing and enough large ones to separate sections.
terms.example: A 4pt base giving 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32 and 40, with nothing in between permitted.

terms.shortDef: Anyone whose work is affected by, or affects, the design.
terms.longDef: Stakeholders include legal, support, operations and engineering as much as executives, and the ones who know most about the constraints are rarely the most senior. Involving them early converts late objections into early requirements. Mapping who decides, who advises and who is merely informed prevents most of the friction.
terms.example: Bringing customer support into a refund redesign early surfaces the three questions every caller actually asks.
terms.misuse: Stakeholder is not a synonym for executive. Treating it that way is how teams discover a legal constraint the week before launch.

terms.shortDef: A result unlikely to be chance alone, given the sample.
terms.longDef: Significance says how surprising your result would be if there were genuinely no difference. It says nothing about how big or valuable the difference is — with enough traffic a meaningless 0.05% lift becomes significant. Always read it alongside the effect size and confidence interval.
terms.example: A 6% lift with a confidence interval spanning −1% to 13% is not yet a result you should ship on.
terms.misuse: "Not significant" does not mean "no difference". It often means the sample was too small to tell.

terms.shortDef: A short comic showing a person's situation before and after.
terms.longDef: Storyboards place a design in the context that surrounds it — where the person is, what interrupted them, what they do next. That context is exactly what a screen mockup omits and where most product ideas fail. Six frames is usually enough, and drawing quality is irrelevant.
terms.example: Four frames showing a parent trying to pay for a school trip on a phone while walking, which rules out a desktop-first flow.

terms.shortDef: The documented rules for how the product should look and sound.
terms.longDef: A style guide records typography, colour, spacing, imagery, logo use and tone of voice, with the reasoning behind each. It is a reference document rather than working code, which is what distinguishes it from a design system. On its own it drifts from the product within a couple of releases.
terms.example: A page defining the type scale, the two permitted weights, and when to use sentence case rather than title case.
terms.misuse: A style guide is not a design system. Guidance without shared components has no mechanism to keep the product in line.

terms.shortDef: The number chosen in advance to judge whether a change worked.
terms.longDef: Declaring it before the work prevents the team picking whichever number moved afterwards. A good one is sensitive enough to move within the measurement window and close enough to user value to be worth moving. Pair it with guardrail metrics so an improvement in one place cannot quietly damage another.
terms.example: "Share of searches ending in a term being opened", agreed before the search redesign began.
terms.misuse: Choosing the metric after seeing the results is the most common analytical failure in product work.

terms.shortDef: A fixed set of questions asked of many people at once.
terms.longDef: Surveys are good at measuring how widespread something already is and poor at discovering what it is. They need a defined population, a sample large enough to say anything, and question wording that has been tested on real humans first. Every extra question costs completion rate.
terms.example: After a redesign, a two-question survey measures whether task confidence moved, with an optional free-text box for the reason.
terms.misuse: A survey cannot tell you why. Pair it with interviews or session recordings before acting on a surprising number.

terms.shortDef: Drawing conclusions only from those who made it through.
terms.longDef: Studying the people who completed a flow tells you nothing about the ones who dropped out, and it is the drop-outs who hold the problem. The same trap catches teams who research only long-standing customers. Look for where people leave, then go and find them.
terms.example: Interviewing subscribers about onboarding produces glowing feedback, because everyone who found it confusing never subscribed.

terms.shortDef: Operating a device with one or two physical buttons.
terms.longDef: The system scans through focusable elements and the user selects with a switch, so every extra element in the focus order costs real time. It depends entirely on correct focus order, visible focus and reachable controls. Anything requiring a gesture, a drag or a hover is unavailable without an alternative.
terms.example: Reducing a card from four focusable elements to one, with actions in a menu, halves the time to reach the next card.

terms.shortDef: Turning raw research into findings a team can act on.
terms.longDef: Synthesis is the work between the last session and the first insight: coding notes, clustering, weighing evidence and deciding what the study actually shows. It is where most of a study's value is created or lost. Budget roughly as much time for it as for the sessions themselves.
terms.example: After six sessions the researcher spends two days tagging transcripts before writing three findings, each backed by named participants.

terms.shortDef: A ten-question survey producing one usability score out of 100.
terms.longDef: The same ten statements are asked after every study, alternating positive and negative wording, and scored to a single number. Its value is comparability: the score means little alone but a lot against the same product last quarter or against the published average of around 68. It measures perceived usability, not task success.
terms.example: A team reports SUS at 61 before redesigning navigation and 74 after, with the same tasks and recruiting criteria.
terms.misuse: SUS is not a satisfaction score and not a percentage. Seventy-two out of 100 is not "72% usable".

terms.shortDef: A persistent row of top-level destinations, usually along the bottom.
terms.longDef: Tab bars keep three to five destinations permanently visible and one tap away, which makes the product's shape obvious. They work when the sections are peers and mutually exclusive. Beyond five items labels stop fitting and the bar becomes a row of guesses.
terms.example: Search, Browse, Revise and Saved, each with an icon and a label, with the current tab marked by more than colour.
terms.misuse: Tabs are for switching between places, not for actions. A tab that opens a modal breaks the model.

terms.shortDef: The share of participants who completed a task correctly.
terms.longDef: The most basic usability metric: did they get there, unaided, with the right outcome. Success has to be defined before the study, including whether partial success counts. It is easy to measure and easy to inflate by writing tasks that hint at the answer.
terms.example: Nine of twelve participants reached the confirmation screen without help, giving a 75% success rate.
terms.misuse: A high success rate with long, painful sessions is not a good result. Read it next to time on task and error counts.

terms.shortDef: The agreed set of categories and terms for classifying content.
terms.longDef: A taxonomy fixes what the categories are and what each is called, so that content, filters, search and analytics all speak the same language. It usually needs to accommodate items belonging in more than one place. Its hardest part is not the structure but agreeing the words with everyone who uses them.
terms.example: Settling that a garment is tagged "outerwear" rather than "coats" or "jackets", everywhere, including in the filters.
terms.misuse: A taxonomy is not the same as a sitemap. One classifies content; the other describes the pages you built from it.

terms.shortDef: Future cost created by choosing a faster solution now.
terms.longDef: Some debt is deliberate and sensible — ship now, refactor after the experiment resolves — and some accumulates through neglect. Either way the interest shows up as slower delivery and more bugs. For designers it matters because it explains why a small visual change is quoted at three weeks.
terms.example: Three separate form implementations mean one validation change has to be made and tested three times.

terms.shortDef: Code that records what happens in a product.
terms.longDef: Events have to be designed: what is captured, what it is named, what properties travel with it, and what is deliberately not collected. Poorly planned instrumentation produces data nobody can answer a question with, and often more personal data than intended. Deciding the question first is what makes the event useful.
terms.example: Recording that a search returned no results, with the query length but not the query itself, when privacy requires it.
terms.misuse: Tracking everything "in case we need it" creates a privacy liability and a dataset too noisy to analyse.

terms.shortDef: Every process has complexity that cannot be removed, only moved.
terms.longDef: Some complexity is inherent to the problem, and the only question is who absorbs it: the user, the designer or the engineer. Good products push it toward the system — smart defaults, inference, sensible fallbacks — rather than exposing it as another field on a form. Pretending it can be deleted just relocates it somewhere worse.
terms.example: An email client that parses "lunch Thursday 1pm" absorbs the complexity of date entry instead of showing three dropdowns.
terms.misuse: Not an excuse for a complicated interface. The law says complexity must be handled, not displayed.

terms.shortDef: Letting users increase line, word and letter spacing without breakage.
terms.longDef: WCAG requires that content still work when line height is raised to 1.5 times the font size, paragraph spacing to twice, letter spacing to 0.12 and word spacing to 0.16. People with dyslexia and low vision use these settings routinely. Layouts built on fixed heights fail this immediately.
terms.example: A card whose height grows with its content rather than clipping the third line when spacing increases.

terms.shortDef: Swapping a design's values without changing its components.
terms.longDef: Theming works when components read semantic tokens rather than literal values, so light, dark, high-contrast or brand variants are configuration rather than forks. The hard part is naming: tokens must describe role, not appearance. A theme that requires component changes is not a theme.
terms.example: One Button component rendering correctly in light, dark and a partner's brand palette with no conditional code.

terms.shortDef: Asking participants to narrate their thoughts while working.
terms.longDef: Participants say what they are looking at, expecting and deciding as they go. It exposes the reasoning behind a click, which no analytics event can give you. Talking does slow people down and can make them more deliberate than usual, so timing data from a think-aloud session is not a clean benchmark.
terms.example: "I'm looking for the total… I assume this arrow opens the breakdown… no, that collapsed the whole thing."
terms.misuse: Retrospective think-aloud, where people narrate after the fact, is a different method — it protects timing data but relies on memory.

terms.shortDef: The part of a phone screen a thumb reaches comfortably.
terms.longDef: Holding a phone one-handed leaves a natural arc near the bottom and the holding side easy to reach, and the far top corner hard. Frequent and primary actions belong in the easy zone; destructive ones benefit from being harder to hit. Grip varies by hand size and by whether the person is walking, so treat it as a tendency rather than a map.
terms.example: Putting the main action bar at the bottom of a tall screen rather than in a top-right corner nobody can reach.

terms.shortDef: How long participants take to complete a defined task.
terms.longDef: Timing is meaningful for tasks people want over with — finding a phone number, paying a bill — and misleading for tasks people enjoy, where longer may be better. Only count successful attempts, or a fast failure will flatter the average. Report the median, since one lost participant can double a mean.
terms.example: Median time to add a payment card fell from 96 to 54 seconds after the form was reordered.
terms.misuse: Do not compare times from a think-aloud session with silent ones. Narrating slows people down by design.

terms.shortDef: A brief message confirming something happened.
terms.longDef: A toast appears without taking focus, states an outcome and disappears. It suits confirmations and low-stakes information, sometimes with a single action such as undo. Anything the user must act on, or must be able to re-read, belongs somewhere persistent — a toast is gone in seconds and invisible to a screen reader unless announced.
terms.example: "Saved." appearing above the tab bar after a save, paired with a live-region announcement.
terms.misuse: Errors in a toast are a common failure. If the user has to fix something, the message must stay on screen.

terms.shortDef: A small label revealed on hover or focus explaining a control.
terms.longDef: Tooltips supplement a control that is already understandable, adding detail for those who want it. They fail on touch, where there is no hover, and they hide information behind an interaction that many users never perform. Anything essential should be visible instead.
terms.example: Hovering a chart legend reveals the exact definition of the metric, which is also stated in the report below.
terms.misuse: A tooltip is not a fix for an unlabelled icon. If the icon needs explaining, it needs a label.

terms.shortDef: The area that responds to a tap, which is larger than the icon.
terms.longDef: Platform guidance puts the minimum at around 44 by 44 points on iOS and 48 by 48 density-independent pixels on Android, and WCAG 2.2 sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels as an absolute floor for the web. The visible mark can be smaller than the target — padding and hit slop extend the area without adding visual weight. Adjacent targets also need space between them.
terms.example: A 16px close icon inside a 44pt tappable area, with 8pt of clearance from the control beside it.
terms.misuse: Sizing the target to the icon is one of the most common mobile defects, and it disproportionately affects people with tremor.

terms.shortDef: Any point where a person interacts with a service.
terms.longDef: Touchpoints include the app, the email, the letter, the call centre and the physical shop — anywhere the organisation meets the person. Experience quality is set by the worst one and by the joins between them, not by the best. Most journey mapping exists to make the joins visible.
terms.example: A booking confirmation email that uses different reference numbers from the app is a broken join between two touchpoints.

terms.shortDef: Uniform spacing applied across a run of letters.
terms.longDef: Tracking is adjusted for optical reasons: large display text usually needs slight negative tracking, and small uppercase labels need positive tracking to stay readable. Body text almost never needs any. It differs from kerning, which adjusts the space between one specific pair of letters.
terms.example: A 34px serif headword set at −0.6 tracking, and a 13px uppercase label opened up to +0.6.
terms.misuse: Tracking and kerning are often conflated. Kerning is per-pair and usually the typeface's job, not yours.

terms.shortDef: A full text version of audio or video content.
terms.longDef: A transcript can be read at the reader's pace, searched, translated and used with a braille display, which captions cannot. For video it should describe important visual information as well as speech. It is often the cheapest accessibility improvement for content-heavy products, and it helps search too.
terms.example: A recorded research readout published with a transcript, so a finding can be found by searching for a phrase.

terms.shortDef: Testing whether people can find things in a bare navigation structure.
terms.longDef: Participants are shown the hierarchy as plain text — no visual design, no search — and asked where they would look for a given item. Stripping the interface isolates the labels and structure from everything else. The output is a success rate and a map of where people went wrong.
terms.example: Asked to find the returns policy, 40% of participants open "Orders" and only 22% reach "Help → Deliveries and returns".

terms.shortDef: Deep in one discipline, competent across several others.
terms.longDef: The vertical stroke is your depth — the thing you are genuinely expert in — and the horizontal is enough breadth to collaborate credibly with adjacent disciplines. It describes what most product teams want: someone who can carry their own craft and speak engineering, research and content. Breadth without depth makes you replaceable; depth without breadth makes you hard to work with.
terms.example: An interaction designer who can read a component's code, write clear microcopy and run a usability test.

terms.shortDef: The fixed set of text sizes a design is allowed to use.
terms.longDef: Choosing five or six sizes with meaningful gaps between them creates hierarchy that holds across a whole product, and removes a decision from every screen. Steps that are too close read as accidents; steps that are too far apart leave nothing usable in the middle. The scale should be defined as tokens so nothing can quietly introduce a seventh size.
terms.example: 13, 15, 17, 22 and 34, where 15 is list text, 17 is prose and 34 is reserved for the headword.
terms.misuse: A scale generated from a mathematical ratio still needs judgement. Rounding to whole pixels and checking each step in situ matters more than the formula.

terms.shortDef: A designed set of letterforms; a font is one instance of it.
terms.longDef: The typeface is the design — Inter, Fraunces, Georgia — while a font is a specific weight, style and size of it. The distinction survives from metal type, where each size was physically separate. Choosing one is a legibility decision before it is an aesthetic one: x-height, character width and how easily similar shapes are told apart.
terms.example: Fraunces is the typeface; Fraunces SemiBold Italic at 34pt is a font.
terms.misuse: The words are used interchangeably in everyday conversation, but in a type conversation the distinction still carries weight.

terms.shortDef: Someone focused on the visual and interactive surface of a product.
terms.longDef: UI design covers layout, typography, colour, iconography, states and the components a product is built from, usually within a design system. It is a craft discipline requiring real depth in visual communication, not a decorative step after the thinking. In smaller teams the same person also does the UX work, which is where the titles blur.
terms.example: Defining every state of a form field, checking contrast in both themes, and adding it to the component library.
terms.misuse: "Just make it pretty" misunderstands the role: hierarchy, contrast and state design are usability work.

terms.shortDef: Letting people reverse an action instead of confirming it first.
terms.longDef: Undo turns a decision into something recoverable, which lets the interface stop interrupting with confirmations. It is faster for the common case and safer for the mistaken one. It needs a clear window, a visible offer, and genuine reversal — not a message claiming reversal that only hides the change.
terms.example: Deleting an email removes it immediately and offers "Undo" for a few seconds, rather than asking "are you sure?" every time.
terms.misuse: Undo cannot cover everything. Truly irreversible actions — sending money, publishing — still need confirmation.

terms.shortDef: Participants complete tasks alone while software records them.
terms.longDef: A platform delivers the tasks, records screen and voice, and returns the sessions for review. It scales to dozens of participants across time zones for the cost of one moderated study. The trade is that you cannot ask a follow-up question, so the task wording has to be unambiguous before you launch.
terms.example: A team posts a five-task study to a research panel overnight and reviews twenty recordings the next morning.

terms.shortDef: Watching real people attempt real tasks with your design.
terms.longDef: You give a participant a task, then stay quiet and watch where they hesitate, backtrack or give up. The output is a list of observed problems, not opinions about whether people liked it. Five or six participants per audience usually surfaces most of the serious issues, which is why teams run small tests often rather than one big study a year.
terms.example: Before shipping a new checkout, a team asks eight shoppers to buy a specific pair of shoes and counts how many reach confirmation without help.
terms.misuse: Not the same as a focus group. Usability testing observes one person doing a task; a focus group collects group opinions, which are a poor predictor of behaviour.

terms.shortDef: A diagram of the steps and decisions to complete a task.
terms.longDef: Flows show screens as nodes and decisions as branches, which makes missing states and dead ends visible before anything is designed. They are the fastest way to agree scope with engineering, because every branch is work. Keeping them at the level of decisions rather than screens keeps them readable.
terms.example: A password reset flow showing the branch where the email is not recognised, which the happy-path design had ignored.
terms.misuse: A flow is not a sitemap. One describes movement through a task, the other the structure of the content.

terms.shortDef: A structured conversation to understand someone's context and goals.
terms.longDef: You ask about what someone did, when and why, and follow the answers rather than a script. Interviews are strong on motivation and history and weak on prediction — people are poor forecasters of their own future behaviour. Ask about the last time something happened rather than what they would usually do.
terms.example: Instead of "would you pay for this?", ask "walk me through the last time you paid for a tool like this."
terms.misuse: An interview is not a usability test. Asking someone's opinion of a screen tells you far less than watching them use it.

terms.shortDef: A one-sentence unit of work framed around a user's goal.
terms.longDef: Usually written as "As a [role], I want [something], so that [outcome]", it exists to hold a conversation rather than to replace one. The "so that" clause is the part that matters and the part most often dropped. Stories are sized to fit in a sprint, which makes them a planning unit, not a design brief.
terms.example: "As a returning customer, I want my last address offered, so that I do not retype it on a phone."
terms.misuse: A story is not a specification. Anything not discussed will be interpreted by whoever picks it up.

terms.shortDef: Someone responsible for how a product works for its users.
terms.longDef: The scope varies more than any other title in the field: some UX designers run research and information architecture, others produce screens. What is consistent is responsibility for the experience of using the thing, rather than only its appearance. Read the job description rather than the title, and ask what the last three projects actually involved.
terms.example: One posting means research, flows and prototypes; another means visual design in an existing design system.
terms.misuse: UX and UI are not two halves of one job. UI is one discipline within a broader practice that includes research and structure.

terms.shortDef: Someone who plans and runs studies to answer product questions.
terms.longDef: Researchers choose methods, recruit appropriately, run studies without leading participants, and turn findings into decisions the team acts on. The hardest parts are usually choosing the right question and getting the results used, not running the sessions. In teams without a researcher, designers do this work with varying rigour.
terms.example: Turning "is the new flow better?" into a benchmark comparing task success across two matched groups.

terms.shortDef: Checking input and telling the user about problems.
terms.longDef: Validate on blur rather than on every keystroke, so people are not told they are wrong while still typing. Confirm success quietly and describe failure specifically, next to the field. Server-side checks still have to run — client-side validation is a convenience, never the guarantee.
terms.example: Leaving the email field with "name@" shows "That address is missing everything after the @" beneath it.
terms.misuse: Validating as the user types marks a half-entered value as an error, which reads as the interface arguing with you.

terms.shortDef: Why someone would choose this over the alternatives.
terms.longDef: A value proposition names the audience, the job, the benefit and the reason to believe it, in language the audience would use. Its test is whether a customer could repeat it back. Most weak ones describe features or list adjectives instead of stating what changes for the person.
terms.example: "Look up any UX term and understand it in under ten seconds, offline" states audience, job and benefit.
terms.misuse: "The leading platform for modern teams" says nothing that a competitor could not also claim.

terms.shortDef: A number that looks good but cannot change a decision.
terms.longDef: Cumulative totals, raw page views and app downloads all rise regardless of whether anything improved, which makes them comfortable to report and useless to act on. The test is whether a movement would change what you do next. Replace them with rates, cohorts and outcomes.
terms.example: "Two million downloads" says nothing; "32% of installs return in week two" is a number you can work with.

terms.shortDef: The order in which a layout leads the eye through content.
terms.longDef: Size, weight, colour, position and space combine to say what matters most, second and third. A page where everything is emphasised has no hierarchy, and one where nothing is has the same problem. The test is whether someone glancing for two seconds takes away the thing you intended.
terms.example: A term page where the headword dominates, the one-line definition is next, and metadata sits quietly beneath both.
terms.misuse: Hierarchy is not just font size. Space and position often do more work than making something bigger.

terms.shortDef: The consistent personality of a product, adjusted to context.
terms.longDef: Voice is constant — the character the product always has. Tone shifts with the situation: the same product is warm in a welcome and plain in a payment failure. Documenting both, with examples of what each sounds like in an error, is what keeps a large team consistent.
terms.example: A playful voice still writes "Your payment did not go through" rather than attempting a joke at that moment.
terms.misuse: Applying one tone everywhere is the common failure. Cheerfulness during a failure reads as indifference.

terms.shortDef: Operating an interface by speaking the names of controls.
terms.longDef: Users say what they see — "tap Save term" — so the accessible name must contain the visible label. Controls with no visible text need a spoken alternative, and numbered overlays are the fallback when nothing matches. It is one of the strongest arguments for labelling icons.
terms.example: "Tap Saved" works because the tab's accessible name starts with the word printed beneath it.
terms.misuse: Giving an element an accessible name that differs from its visible label breaks voice control even though it reads fine.

terms.shortDef: An interface operated and answered by speech.
terms.longDef: Speech has no visible state and no scrollback, so working memory carries everything and answers must be short. Error recovery is the core design problem: what happens when the system mishears, and how the user corrects it without repeating the whole request. Voice excels hands-free and struggles with anything requiring comparison.
terms.example: "Set a reminder for seven" answered with "Reminder at seven this evening — is that right?" rather than silent action.

terms.shortDef: The item that differs from its neighbours is the one remembered.
terms.longDef: When several similar things sit together, the odd one out gets attention and is recalled better. It is the mechanism behind a single filled primary button among outlined ones, or one highlighted pricing tier. Its power is finite: emphasise two things and you have emphasised nothing.
terms.example: A pricing table where only the middle plan has a border and a label pulls most of the clicks to that plan.
terms.misuse: Difference must not be carried by colour alone, or the effect disappears for anyone who cannot distinguish it.

terms.shortDef: The international standard for accessible digital content.
terms.longDef: WCAG organises testable success criteria under four principles and three conformance levels: A, AA and AAA. Most laws and procurement policies reference level AA, which is the practical target. Version 2.2 added criteria on focus appearance, dragging alternatives and minimum target size.
terms.example: Meeting AA means 4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus, keyboard operability and no keyboard traps, among others.
terms.misuse: Passing an automated checker is not conformance. Automated tools catch perhaps a third of the criteria.

terms.shortDef: The empty area around and between elements.
terms.longDef: Space groups, separates and creates emphasis, and it does so faster than borders or colour. Micro white space — inside and between components — drives legibility; macro white space drives the sense of calm and hierarchy. It is the first thing sacrificed under pressure and the first thing that should not be.
terms.example: Doubling the gap between form sections while halving the gap between a label and its field makes the grouping unambiguous.
terms.misuse: White space does not have to be white. It is any unoccupied area, including over a dark background or an image.

terms.shortDef: A stray single line or word left alone by a text break.
terms.longDef: A widow is a last line stranded at the top of a column; an orphan is a first line stranded at the bottom. In interfaces the common version is a single word left on the last line of a heading. Non-breaking spaces and balanced text wrapping fix most cases without manual intervention.
terms.example: A three-word button label breaking so the last word sits alone, fixed by keeping the final two words together.

terms.shortDef: A layout sketch showing structure and priority, not visual design.
terms.longDef: Wireframes answer what goes on the screen, in what order and at what relative importance, using boxes and placeholder text. Keeping them grey and rough is deliberate: it directs feedback to structure rather than to colour choices. They are fastest to change and therefore the right place to argue about hierarchy.
terms.example: A grey block for the hero, a stack of labelled rectangles for the product list, and a note reading "filters, 6 max".
terms.misuse: A wireframe is not a low-quality mockup. It is a different question — structure, not appearance — and adding colour undermines it.

terms.shortDef: A person secretly performs what the system is meant to do.
terms.longDef: Participants believe they are using a working product while a researcher behind the scenes produces the responses. It lets you test an experience that would be expensive to build — a recommendation engine, a voice assistant, anything with a model behind it — before committing to building it. The illusion has to hold, including the delays, or people adjust their behaviour to the human.
terms.example: Testing an assistant by having a researcher type the replies, to learn what people actually ask before any model is chosen.
terms.misuse: It is not a shortcut to a demo. The point is observing unprompted behaviour, which means the participant must not know.

terms.shortDef: A structured working session with a defined output.
terms.longDef: A workshop differs from a meeting by having activities, a facilitator and something concrete produced by the end. It is the right tool when a decision needs several people's knowledge, and the wrong one when a decision needs a single owner. Preparation cost is high and usually underestimated.
terms.example: A two-hour session where engineering, support and design map the refund journey and mark the three worst moments.
terms.misuse: Not a substitute for research. A room full of colleagues guessing is still guessing, however well facilitated.

terms.shortDef: The height of a lowercase x, which drives apparent size.
terms.longDef: Two typefaces set at the same point size can look very different because their x-heights differ. A large x-height generally reads better at small sizes and on screens, which is why interface faces tend to have one. It also means point size alone is not comparable between families.
terms.example: Inter at 15px appears noticeably larger than Garamond at 15px, because its lowercase letters are taller.

terms.shortDef: Unfinished tasks stay in mind more than completed ones.
terms.longDef: An interrupted or incomplete task keeps a foothold in memory until it is resolved. Progress indicators, partially filled profiles and unfinished checklists all exploit this, creating a mild pull back to the product. Used heavily it becomes a nag, and people resolve the tension by leaving.
terms.example: A profile showing "60% complete" draws people back to fill in the remaining fields more than a plain edit link does.
terms.misuse: Not a licence for permanent unread badges. Manufactured incompleteness reads as pressure, not as helpfulness.
